title: Purpose, Execution, Judgement: A Framework for Human-AI Collaboration and Organisational AI Capability in the Post-ChatGPT Era

detail.title: Purpose, Execution, Judgement: A Framework for Human-AI Collaboration and Organisational AI Capability in the Post-ChatGPT Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and CEO of Dixon AI Ltd, an AI consultancy and training provider. The frameworks discussed in this paper are used in the author's commercial consultancy practice.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces and integrates two complementary frameworks for understanding human-AI collaboration in the post-ChatGPT era. The Purpose, Execution, Judgement (PEJ) framework delineates how humans and artificial intelligence share productive work: humans define Purpose (why), collaborate with AI on Execution (how), and apply Judgement (which output matters). The AI Capability framework defines organisational readiness as a multiplicative function of five factors: Talent, Purpose, AI Literacy, AI Tools, and Data Infrastructure. Independently, PEJ answers how humans and AI collaborate while AI Capability answers what organisations need to make that collaboration effective. This paper argues that integrating the two yields a more complete theory of AI-enabled value creation. Drawing on recent empirical evidence of generative AI productivity effects, systematic reviews of human-AI collaboration taxonomies, and Industry 5.0 principles, the paper positions PEJ and AI Capability against the existing literature, identifies gaps in current frameworks, and advances six formal propositions for future research. Implications for organisational design, leadership practice, workforce development, and educational reform are discussed. The paper contributes to the emerging field of human-AI teaming by offering a practitioner-accessible yet theoretically grounded model that scales from individual task to enterprise transformation.

detail.title: Markets for (concealable) Information

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 08/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study markets in which imperfectly informed experts occasionally receive signals about an unknown state and sell their expertise to decision makers. Experts care both about profits and about influencing decisions toward a preferred action. Potential customers have heterogeneous idiosyncratic biases favoring a particular action, but they also value matching their action to the true state. We show that, in a monopoly market with uniformly distributed decision maker biases, an expert has no incentive to filter information, even when biased. However, when decision maker biases are not uniformly distributed, filtering becomes an instrument of influence, and the optimal filtering depends on whether the distribution is moderate or polarized. Similarly, if influence requires securing a majority rather than maximizing overall support, the monopolist trades off profits against the probability of gaining the required majority. In a duopoly, we characterize how purchasing decisions depend on expert biases and signal quality. The total amount of information purchased can be non-monotonic in the preferences of decision makers. By contrast, when experts do not value influence and disclose truthfully, any equilibrium requires that decision makers either purchase from both experts or from none. Our results shed light on information provision in media markets and, more broadly, on competition among biased experts seeking to influence decisions.

detail.title: Strategic Analysis and Growth Priorities of Veralab

detail.abstract: This report analyzes Veralab, an Italian beauty brand that has undergone substantial growth in recent years. Such expansion is noteworthy not only for its economic outcomes, but also for the way the brand has constructed and communicated its image. The brand has also invested heavily in digital communication, community engagement, and a narrative built around authenticity, which seem to have supported its growth alongside economic performance. To examine this more closely, the report makes use of frameworks such as PESTEL and Porter's Five Forces, together with an assessment of the company's internal resources. These tools help structure the discussion, although they are not applied in a purely mechanical way. Instead, they serve as a way to connect industry-level pressures with the specific strategic decisions the company appears to have made over time. An important element in Veralab's growth is its strong founder-led identity and its direct-to-consumer model. Customer engagement appears to play a key role in sustaining brand loyalty and differentiation. However, rapid expansion also raises questions. Scaling operations, managing increasing organizational complexity, and approaching international markets carefully will likely become more demanding over time. Instead of presenting a fixed business plan, this report offers a strategic assessment grounded in academic theory but attentive to practical realities. Ultimately, it aims to better understand how modern beauty brands pursue growth while trying to preserve coherence and brand credibility-something that is often easier said than done.

title: When Aggregate Tradeoffs Mask Individual Alignment: Evidence from Follower-Targeted Recommendation
affiliations: Peking University,  and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: When Aggregate Tradeoffs Mask Individual Alignment: Evidence from Follower-Targeted Recommendation
detail.abstract: Content-sharing platforms are often characterized by an engagement–growth tradeoff in recommendation design. Delivering content to existing followers generates reliable engagement, but consumes capacity that could expose creators to new audiences and fuel ecosystem expansion. Using a large-scale randomized experiment on a major short-video platform, we confirm this tension at the aggregate level: blocking follower-targeted delivery reduces engagement while modestly increasing follower acquisition. However, we show that this apparent tradeoff largely disappears at the creator level. Heterogeneous treatment effects reveal two patterns: negative impacts on engagement are widespread but highly concentrated in magnitude; creators who are most harmed in engagement are on average also harmed in growth. Thus, the aggregate exploitation–exploration tension does not generally manifest as a pervasive individual-level conflict. We further demonstrate that observable scale metrics such as follower count fail to reliably identify highly-impacted creators. By combining randomized experimentation with double machine learning, we recover creator-level causal dependence and construct targeting rules that substantially outperform scale-based heuristics. To translate heterogeneous effects into operational policy, we formalize recommendation design as a constrained welfare maximization problem under limited exposure capacity. Because heterogeneous engagement and growth effects are strongly aligned, the multi-objective allocation problem effectively reduces to a single-index rule at empirically relevant protection levels. Engagement-based targeting achieves welfare statistically indistinguishable from explicit multi-objective optimization. Our findings suggest that aggregate engagement–growth tradeoffs may not imply structural conflict, and that alignment in heterogeneous effects enables platforms to simultaneously protect vulnerable creators and foster ecosystem expansion through data-driven allocation.

title: Applying Aspects of Disability Determination Methods from the Netherlands in the United States
affiliations: Harvard Medical School - Department of Health Care Policy, University of Oregon and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE)

detail.title: Applying Aspects of Disability Determination Methods from the Netherlands in the United States
detail.abstract: In contrast to the disability determination process in the United States, the Netherlands uses a unique method that directly measures an applicant's residual work capacity following the onset of a health condition. Standardized measures of functional abilities are linked to the requirements of actual jobs in the Netherlands, allowing for direct computation of a set of feasible jobs and the resulting estimated residual earnings capacity of an applicant, conditional on skills. In this article, we explain the measurement of work capacity in the Netherlands and then apply aspects of that method to estimate work capacity in a representative sample of U.S. working-age adults. We find that 11.8 percent of U.S. adults aged 18–65 have estimated earnings capacity below the substantial gainful activity threshold for U.S. Disability Insurance benefits. On average, compared with individuals with at least a bachelor's degree, individuals with less education have more functional limitations, a smaller set of feasible occupations, and lower estimated earnings capacity.

title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, , Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc., , Lyft, Inc., Lyft, Inc. and Lyft, Inc.

detail.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This work is done when the second author was a faculty advisor at Lyft Inc.

detail.abstract:
Ride-hailing platforms increasingly rely on non-exclusive notifications—broadcasting a single request to multiple drivers simultaneously—to mitigate the inefficiencies caused by uncertain driver acceptance. In this paper, we formally model the Notification Set Selection Problem for a single decision cycle, where the platform must determine the optimal subset of drivers to notify for each incoming ride request. We analyze this combinatorial optimization problem under two distinct contention-resolution protocols: First Acceptance (FA), which prioritizes speed by assigning the ride to the first responder, and Best Acceptance (BA), which prioritizes match quality by selecting the highest-valued driver among those who accept.

We establish that welfare maximization under both mechanisms is strongly NP-hard, effectively ruling out the existence of a Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS). Despite this intractability, we derive several positive algorithmic results. For the FA protocol, we present a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for the single-rider case and a constant-factor approximation (with factor 4) for the general matching setting. We highlight that the FA valuation function can be viewed as a novel discrete choice model with theoretical properties of independent interest. For the BA mechanism, we show that the objective function is monotone and submodular, admitting a standard (1 - 1/e)-approximation. Furthermore, by establishing a polynomial-time demand oracle, we demonstrate that it is possible to surpass the (1 - 1/e) barrier. Finally, in the special case of homogeneous acceptance probabilities, we prove that the BA problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time via a linear programming formulation.

title: Minimum Viable Equivalence Packs: An Institutional Diligence Framework for Tokenized Products

detail.title: Minimum Viable Equivalence Packs: An Institutional Diligence Framework for Tokenized Products

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: Consent
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract:
When Circle disclosed $3.3 billion in USDC reserves at Silicon Valley Bank on March 10, 2023, every tier label, attestation report, and “institutional grade” designation failed to surface the exposure. USDC traded at $0.87. The episode revealed that tokenized product diligence lacks a common standard: rights parity, custody segregation, system-of-record primacy, and insolvency treatment were each unexamined or untested at the moment they mattered most.

This paper develops the Minimum Viable Equivalence Pack (MVEP), a nine-category institutional diligence framework that specifies the minimum artifacts, observable metrics, and pass/fail tests required to clear a risk committee’s threshold for any tokenized product. The framework decomposes equivalence into three independently testable claims: legal (rights, priority, enforceability), operational (system of record, reconciliation, exception handling), and economic (settlement finality inclusive of value integrity and convertibility). A product can satisfy one dimension while failing another; the SVB weekend broke all three simultaneously.

The MVEP is applied to two asset classes where institutional volume is concentrating: tokenized Treasury bills and money market fund shares (where records integrity and settlement finality dominate) and tokenized private credit (where rights enforcement and servicing continuity dominate). For composed products, equivalence degrades to the weakest layer. The paper introduces continuous monitoring through the Control Layer Intensity Index (CLII), a scoring methodology originally developed for stablecoin gateway infrastructure, extended here to custody segregation, reconciliation integrity, and concentration risk across tokenized products. The MVEP is designed to be wrong in known ways: its value lies in making the standard explicit, the gaps visible, and the failure modes predictable.

title: Measurement-Corrected ESG Scores: Unveiling the True Cost of Debt and Asset Pricing Implications with Deep Learning
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Measurement-Corrected ESG Scores: Unveiling the True Cost of Debt and Asset Pricing Implications with Deep Learning
detail.abstract: This dissertation studies how measurement error in ESG ratings distorts financial inference and proposes a machine-learning framework to recover the latent sustainability signal. The global sustainable investment market exceeds $ trillion, yet ESG measurement remains critically flawed. We introduce EthosChain, a hybrid deep learning architecture (TCN + Multi-Head Attention) trained on semi-synthetic data that filters out noise and persistent firm-specific bias, producing a measurementcorrected ESG score (DAI-ESG). Using this score, we show: (i) DAI-ESG predicts future bond spreads with % higher accuracy than traditional scores; (ii) a one-standarddeviation increase in DAI-ESG causes a-basis point reduction in the cost of debt-an effect % larger than OLS estimates using traditional scores, confirming substantial attenuation bias; (iii) this effect operates through reduced information asymmetry (%) and lower default risk (%); (iv) DAI-ESG is a priced factor in equity markets (. % annualized alpha), and factor spanning tests confirm it is not subsumed by existing green, carbon, or ESG factors; (v) it outperforms experienced human analysts by % in predicting credit spread changes; and (vi) it anticipates major ESGrelated shocks up to months in advance. A natural experiment using the EU Non-Financial Reporting Directive confirms the causal interpretation. However, we also identify boundary conditions: the effect weakens for firms with thin information environments (small firms, low news coverage). Theoretically, we propose that any asset pricing or corporate finance relation estimated with noisy sustainability measures may be systematically biased, and traditional econometric fixes cannot fully eliminate this bias. Practical takeaways: Banks can integrate DAI-ESG directly into credit risk models to reduce default rates by basis points and increase risk-adjusted returns by %, while investors can use it to avoid impending ESG shocks and enhance portfolio performance. All empirical results are fully reproducible using the provided replication package, available at GitHub Repository Link.

detail.title: Women's empowerment and nutrition: Evidence from rural households in Africa and Asia

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEF – Discussion Papers on Development Policy No. 366, 2026; Center for Development Research, Bonn (https://doi.org/10.48565/bonndoc-776)

detail.abstract: Women play key roles in food systems, yet continue to face persistent disadvantages in terms of low decision-making power and limited access to goods, services, and markets. Discrimination against women is often deeply ingrained in social norms, policies, and institutions. Widely observed gender gaps are not only unfair; they also undermine broader sustainability objectives. Extensive evidence shows that women's empowerment contributes to productivity, efficiency, and broader social welfare gains. We review and synthesize the literature on links between women's empowerment and nutrition, focusing on rural households in Africa and Asia. We analyze advances in the measurement of women's empowerment, discuss strengths and limitations of existing metrics, and summarize the broad empirical evidence showing that women's empowerment is positively associated with dietary quality and nutrition. Further, we develop a conceptual framework, highlighting key mechanisms of the empowerment-nutrition relationship, including women's bargaining power, control over income, and time allocation. Using this framework and examples from different countries, we show that development initiatives, such as promoting agricultural commercialization and women's off-farm employment, can involve tradeoffs, sometimes resulting in undesirable empowerment and/or nutrition outcomes. Such tradeoffs need to be properly understood and addressed through gender-transformative policies. We conclude by discussing policy and research implications.

title: Operational Risk in Token Economies: How Infrastructure Failures Strengthen Adaptive Controllers and Break Reputation Systems

detail.title: Operational Risk in Token Economies: How Infrastructure Failures Strengthen Adaptive Controllers and Break Reputation Systems

detail.abstract: When a token network's adaptive reward controller mistakes a temporary infrastructure outage for a permanent loss of operators, it over-compensates with higher rewards. This over-reaction accidentally builds a financial buffer that protects the network when a real economic shock arrives. This counterintuitive finding emerges from a 624-run agent-based simulation of a DePIN token economy extended with an operational risk layer (infrastructure outages, key losses, correlated software failures, and regulatory disruptions) calibrated to empirical failure rates across Ethereum, Helium, Geodnet, and Filecoin. Under competitor shock, the adaptive controller reduces worst-case outcome variance by 6.89×, up from 6.25× without operational risk. The analytical prediction was that infrastructure failures would make the controller less effective at stabilizing the network; instead, they make it more effective. Fixedrate reward schedules, which cannot adjust to any source of disruption, perform even worse (outcome variability increases from 0.544 to 0.569), widening the adaptive controller's advantage. A second finding reveals a design vulnerability not apparent from economic-only simulation. Reputation systems that gate recovery on a performance threshold break when routine failures make that threshold unachievable. At 0.5% daily downtime, an operator has only a 16% chance of clearing the recovery threshold in any given quarter. The result: average reputation decays to 0.18 on a 0-5 scale, effectively disabling reputationweighted governance. The collapse is structural; no adjustment to the decay rate fixes it, but lowering the recovery threshold to 0.95 restores stability. The operational risk taxonomy draws on two emerging standards: the Validator Operation Standard (ValOS), with 74 active risk vectors and 64 testable controls, and the Node Operator Risk Standard (NORS), providing institutional certification across 31 control objectives. Lido V3 stVaults, which set each operator's collateral requirements based on their risk score, demonstrate that ValOS-aligned risk assessment already governs economic outcomes on Ethereum mainnet. The simulation methodology provides a template for extending other agent-based token simulations with operational risk.

detail.title: From Pixels to Signals: Hierarchical Vision Transformers for Return Prediction
detail.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that candlestick-chart image predictability weakens in more recent data and remains hard to interpret. Using CRSP U.S. equities (1993-2024), we revisit this claim by comparing a CNN benchmark with a hierarchical vision transformer (Hiera) trained on candlestick-and-volume images. Hiera produces a stronger and more stable cross-sectional return ordering that persists in a post-2019 holdout and survives implementability checks. We develop two diagnostics - controlled synthetic probes and occlusion maps - paired with spanning regressions to characterize the learned signal. The diagnostics constrain interpretation and localize predictive content to patterns near the end of the lookback window.

title: Good Civilizations & Industrialized Societies

detail.title: Good Civilizations & Industrialized Societies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fordham Law Legal Studies Research Paper

detail.abstract: This essay examines two primary references to synthesize views on industrialization and human autonomy. The first, authored by Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi in 1909, is titled Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule. Initially written in Gandhi's native Gujarati and banned by the British as a seditious text in 1910, the book contains views on industrialization and how it could help bring about Swaraj, a term for home-rule coined by Maharshi Dayanand Saraswati, best understood as "India for Indians". The second reference is authored by Theodore John Kaczynski and titled Industrial Society and Its Future. This 35,000-word text argues that industrialization began as a destructive process, forcing humans to create sociopolitical orders that suppress human freedom and potential. Serving as the ideological framework of Kaczynski's 1978-1995 mail bomb campaign, the manuscript was published by the Washington Post after an offer was made to end his bombing campaign in exchange for national exposure of the text. This essay explores only specific portions of Kaczynski's text, namely sections 38 through 42, as they relate surrogate activities to human autonomy.

title: NEW RESEARCH PRACTICES IN THE AI ERA: VALIDATION, DATA GOVERNANCE AND ETHICS WITHIN THE FRAMEWORK OF THE SDGs

detail.title: NEW RESEARCH PRACTICES IN THE AI ERA: VALIDATION, DATA GOVERNANCE AND ETHICS WITHIN THE FRAMEWORK OF THE SDGs
detail.abstract:
The 21st century has marked an irreversible point in the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), research, and education. Multiple studies on artificial intelligence in education (AIIE) have moved from an exploratory phase to one characterized by critical scrutiny and much more rigorous validation. This is due to the very emergence of generative AI; the conversations and debates taking place in academia no longer focus on AI trivialities, but rather on how it can be implemented in an effective, transparent, ethical, and equitable manner (Acuña-Gamboa, 2025).

This chapter delves into the emerging trends that define the new agenda for high-impact research, starting from the premise that the future of research lies not only in technological innovation, but also in building a framework, establishing solid governance, and validating pedagogical and academic benefits. But above all, it requires an unavoidable and inexcusable commitment to equity and reducing the gaps that exacerbate the stark inequalities that, despite all predictions, persist in humanity (Álvarez & Saborío-Taylor, 2025).

To this end, we will explore how the very methodology of scientific research is being redefined by AI, and how inherent challenges persist regarding data processing, algorithmic transparency, ethics, and the pursuit of quality science that contributes to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda. This is because it is no secret that the initial optimism has given way to a skeptical optimism, where the research community faces the dual challenge of measuring the effects of AI on complex competencies and, simultaneously, ensuring that its application in science is rigorous, transparent, and above all, fair.

title: Visioning Human-Agentic AI Teaming: Continuity, Tension, and Future Research
affiliations: Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California, Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems, Arizona State University - W. P. Carey School of Business and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: Visioning Human-Agentic AI Teaming: Continuity, Tension, and Future Research
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is undergoing a structural transformation marked by the rise of agentic systems capable of open-ended action trajectories, generative representations and outputs, and evolving objectives. These properties introduce structural uncertainty into human-AI teaming (HAT), including uncertainty about behavior trajectories, epistemic grounding, and the stability of governing logics over time. Under such conditions, alignment cannot be secured through agreement on bounded outputs; it must be continuously sustained as plans unfold and priorities shift. We advance Team Situation Awareness (Team SA) theory, grounded in shared perception, comprehension, and projection, as an integrative anchor for this transition. While Team SA remains analytically foundational, its stabilizing logic presumes that shared awareness, once achieved, will support coordinated action through iterative updating. Agentic AI challenges this presumption. Our argument unfolds in two stages: first, we extend Team SA to reconceptualize both human and AI awareness under open-ended agency, including the sensemaking of projection congruence across heterogeneous systems. Second, we interrogate whether the dynamic processes traditionally assumed to stabilize teaming in relational interaction, cognitive learning, and coordination and control continue to function under adaptive autonomy. By distinguishing continuity from tension, we clarify where foundational insights hold and where structural uncertainty introduces strain, and articulate a forward-looking research agenda for HAT. We find that under open-ended agency, Team SA processes can produce the opposite of their intended effects: relational legitimacy may rest on epistemic fragility, iterative updating may amplify rather than correct divergence, and shared awareness may coexist with substantive loss of oversight. The central challenge of HAT is not whether humans and AI can agree in the moment, but whether they can remain aligned as futures are continuously generated, revised, enacted, and governed over time.

detail.title: Bagging the Network
detail.abstract: This paper studies parametric estimation and inference in a dyadic network formation model with nontransferable utilities, incorporating observed covariates and unobservable individual fixed effects. We address both theoretical and computational challenges of maximum likelihood estimation in this complex network model by proposing a new bootstrap aggregating (bagging) estimator, which is asymptotically normal, unbiased, and efficient. We extend the approach to estimating average partial effects and analyzing link function misspecification. Simulations demonstrate strong finite-sample performance. Two empirical applications to Nyakatoke risk-sharing networks and Indian microfinance data find insignificant roles of wealth differences in link formation and the strong influence of caste in Indian villages, respectively.

title: Passive Ownership and Market Selection: Evidence from U.S. Zombie Companies

detail.title: Passive Ownership and Market Selection: Evidence from U.S. Zombie Companies
detail.abstract: Using a panel of U.S. public firms (1990-2024), this study examines how the rise of passive ownership distorts market selection, facilitating the creation and survival of zombie firms. To establish causality, I employ a Granular Instrumental Variable (GIV) framework (Gabaix and Koijen, 2024) leveraging idiosyncratic liquidity shocks of the "Big Three". An exogenous increase in passive ownership raises zombie probability through a dual mechanism. First, a governance channel: within-firm estimates reveal passive capital reduces CEO pay-performance sensitivity. This insulates entrenched management to pursue a "quiet life", causally driving a severe deterioration in structural firm productivity. Second, a credit channel: creditors penalize this governance vacuum by demanding higher loan spreads, especially in stable environments where market turbulence cannot substitute for internal monitoring. Finally, survival analysis reveals that passive capital prolongs ongoing zombie spells.

detail.abstract:
This article critiques the widespread use of the terms “facilitative” and “evaluative” to describe mediation techniques.  Despite their popularity in scholarship and practice, these labels are inconsistently defined, frequently misunderstood, and fundamentally flawed.  Drawing on a survey of mediation experts, the article documents significant confusion about how professionals interpret these terms – and how they think that others interpret them.  It builds on Leonard Riskin’s critique of the facilitative-evaluative framework, which shows that the language not only oversimplifies complex processes but also risks confusing parties and undermining informed decision-making.

As an alternative, the article proposes a behavioral vocabulary that reflects mediators’ values and describes their actions in plain language.  It argues that artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as the Real Practice Systems Coach, can promote better communication by using clear terminology.  The article suggests that AI tools might be more effective than traditional human-centered reform efforts in promoting the use of clearer language.  It urges AI developers, writers, educators, and practitioners to support party decision-making by making mediation easier to understand.

detail.abstract: The Anthropic-Pentagon dispute has generated widespread commentary but fundamental confusion about whether contractors can restrict the government's use of their products. This article argues the question is not novel. The scope of permissible restrictions depends on the acquisition pathway, the contract type, and the negotiated terms. The article surveys the principal pathways through which the federal government acquires AI and examines OpenAI's published Pentagon contract language, which adopts an "any lawful use" standard conditioned on existing legal authorities. A critical tension emerges: although the contract facially permits broad use, OpenAI's retained architectural control over its cloud-only deployment and safety infrastructure may impose practical constraints exceeding those Anthropic sought through express contractual restrictions. The article concludes that the public debate has focused on the wrong question. The more consequential governance failure is the government's inability to secure adequate transparency, audit rights, and safeguards when procuring AI through commercial pathways not designed for technologies this complex and consequential.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of the International Council for Small Business, 0[10.1080/26437015.2026.2623452]

detail.abstract: A promising founding team is one of the criteria investors actively look for in new ventures. Research has shown that gender and ethnicity of founders have signaling power with potentially negative consequences for their perceived risk profile related to new venture funding. Yet it is unknown how new venture teams with gender and ethnic diversity or intersectionality impact new venture funding, although the diversity in new venture teams increases steadily. To address this research need, we build on signaling theory to guide our empirical study, based on 2,626 ventures with diverse new venture teams (6,131 founders). Our results show that gender diversity and intersectionality, as reflected by the presence of a female Asian new venture team member, are significantly negatively related to the absolute amount of new venture funding, yet not ethnic diversity. These findings suggest that signals sent by diverse new venture teams have differing effects on funding.

title: Logical Differencing in Dyadic Network Formation Models with Nontransferable Utilities
affiliations: National University of Singapore, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Yale University

detail.title: Logical Differencing in Dyadic Network Formation Models with Nontransferable Utilities
detail.abstract: This paper considers a semiparametric model of dyadic network formation under nontransferable utilities (NTU). Such dyadic links arise frequently in real-world social interactions that require bilateral consent but by their nature induce additive nonseparability. In our model we show how unobserved individual heterogeneity in the network formation model can be canceled out without requiring additive separability. The approach uses a new method we call logical differencing. The key idea is to construct an observable event involving the intersection of two mutually exclusive restrictions-derived based on weak multivariate monotonicity-on the fixed effects. Based on this identification strategy we provide consistent estimators of the network formation model under NTU. Finite-sample performance of our method is analyzed in a simulation study, and an empirical illustration using the risk-sharing network data from Nyakatoke demonstrates that our proposed method is able to obtain economically intuitive estimates.

title: The Delicate Dance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Delicate Dance
detail.abstract: Leadership frameworks are typically additive; lists of qualities to accumulate, behaviours to demonstrate, habits to build. This paper argues for a fundamentally different view: that leadership is a system, and systems work through coherence, not addition. The Delicate Dance framework rests on a foundation of purpose and six interdependent character qualities; Competence, Clarity, Courage, Conviction, Curiosity, and Compassion. Each is non-negotiable. Each is independent in definition and interdependent in operation. The framework introduces resilience as the behaviour of all six qualities across time, and judgement; encompassing context, discernment, awareness, and adaptability; as the meta-capacity that navigates the tensions and virtuous loops between them. Accountability bridges character and execution, returning always to purpose. The paper also addresses two deliberate omissions; confidence and communication; and argues that genuine credibility is earned through character, not performed through manner.

detail.abstract: Despite broad support for sustainability, the transition from linear to circular economic models remains slow and fragmented across industries. Digital technologies such as the metaverse present new opportunities for enabling circular economy (CE) practices, yet their strategic integration within organizational systems is not fully understood. To address this gap, this study proposes and empirically validates a model that explains how metaverse adoption influences CE implementation through the mediating role of Immersive Knowledge Co-Creation (IKCC), and the moderating effect of Open Eco-Innovation Capability (OEIC). Grounded in the knowledge-based view (KBV), interactive learning theory, and dynamic capabilities theory, the research develops a process-driven and capability-oriented framework to explore the mechanisms and boundary conditions for digital-enabled circular transformation. Empirical data were collected from 220 respondents in Germany's advanced manufacturing sector and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results confirm that IKCC significantly mediates the relationship between metaverse adoption and CE implementation, and that this mediated relationship is stronger in firms with high OEIC. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on digital innovation in the CE by highlighting the critical role of immersive collaboration and organizational readiness in driving circular processes.

detail.abstract: This essay examines the rise of "Green Deals" as large-scale state-sponsored active industrial policies to accelerate a transition toward climate neutrality. Building on the concept of mission-oriented innovation policy (MOIP), it documents how environmental and active industrial policies have converged across advanced economies, reshaping the policy toolkit toward direct public investment and publicly supported investment. The essay provides detailed accounts of the European Union's Green Deal and the U.S. counterpart, situating them in the broader political economy of climate policy. It also highlights initiatives in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Sweden, which additionally illustrate Grean Deal initiatives and how the latter national strategies adapt EU-level frameworks and institutional constraints. A comparative analysis underscores key differences between the EU's fragmented, caseby-case approach and the more streamlined but fiscally uncertain U.S. model. The essay concludes by stressing the need for greater scrutiny of these policies, including their economic efficiency and fiscal sustainability.

title: The Role Of Revenue Collections On Economic Growth And Development In South Sudan
affiliations: Nile University

detail.title: The Role Of Revenue Collections On Economic Growth And Development In South Sudan
detail.abstract:
The primary objective of this study was to assess the challenges facing revenue collection in South Sudan, using the National Revenue Authority (NRA) as a case study. Despite gaining independence in 2011, South Sudan continues to grapple with fiscal instability due to an overwhelming reliance on oil revenues, which account for over 90% of the budget, leaving the economy vulnerable to external shocks and neglecting the development of a sustainable non-oil revenue base. The study adopted a quantitative research approach using a descriptive survey design. Primary data was collected through questionnaires administered to 50 respondents, comprising senior management and support staff at the NRA Juba branch, while secondary data was sourced from relevant institutional reports (2018–2021).

The findings revealed that while the NRA is pivotal for funding public services and fostering state stability, it is hindered by significant structural and administrative challenges. Key findings indicate that the revenue system suffers from a lack of institutional autonomy, widespread political interference, overlapping tax jurisdictions between national and state levels, and a reliance on manual collection systems that exacerbate corruption and leakage. Furthermore, the study confirmed that the non-oil sector, particularly agriculture, remains subsistence-based and under-taxed. The study concludes that sustainable economic growth in South Sudan is contingent upon diversifying the revenue base and formalising the fiscal social contract. Recommendations include granting full financial autonomy to the NRA, implementing the digitalisation of revenue collection through a Single Treasury Account (TSA) to curb corruption, resolving intergovernmental fiscal conflicts, and actively investing in infrastructure to boost the non-oil private sector.

title: Impact Of Small And Medium Scale Enterprises (Smes) Financing On Economic Growth In Nigeria
affiliations: Bayero University

detail.title: Impact Of Small And Medium Scale Enterprises (Smes) Financing On Economic Growth In Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Small and Medium-Scale Enterprises (SMEs) financing on economic growth in Nigeria, utilising advanced econometric techniques such as the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test, the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bound test, and various diagnostic tests. The analysis covers key financial variables, including Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Commercial Bank Loans (CBL), Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Development Finance Institutions Funding (DFIF), and Domestic Credit (DCR). The ARDL bound test confirms a significant long-run relationship between these variables and economic growth, while the Error Correction Model (ECM) results indicate a rapid adjustment towards long-run equilibrium. The findings highlight the crucial role of SME financing in promoting sustainable economic development in Nigeria. The study concludes with recommendations for policymakers and stakeholders to enhance access to finance for SMEs, strengthen financial institutions, and promote good corporate governance practices to harness the full potential of SMEs in contributing to the nation's economic prosperity.

title: Regime-Conditional Risk in U.S. High Yield Credit An Empirical Scenario-Grade Implementation of the Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model

detail.title: Regime-Conditional Risk in U.S. High Yield Credit An Empirical Scenario-Grade Implementation of the Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model
detail.abstract: This paper presents a scenario-grade forward risk framework for U.S. High Yield (HY) credit within the architecture of the Dominant Dynamics Equilibrium Model (DDEM). Rather than generating point forecasts, the analysis focuses on regime-dependent conditional risk behavior under a frozen calibration protocol and a set of validated baseline configurations. Using weekly option-adjusted spread data from 2000-2025, two baseline states are identified through robust statistical matching: MAIN (longer calibration window) and TACTICAL (short-window sensitivity). Forward simulations are conducted over a 52-week horizon using Monte Carlo ensembles (M = 1000 per scenario) across four configurations: no-shock, mild, base, and severe. The results display monotonic scaling in maximum drawdown, stress frequency, panic activation, and recovery time as shock intensity increases. Gaussian mixture diagnostics indicate a unimodal drawdown structure under the MAIN no-shock configuration, whereas the TACTICAL base configuration reveals a statistically supported but low-weight secondary regime, consistent with localized tail sensitivity rather than persistent structural bifurcation. An ancillary fragility proxy is introduced and validated through regime-based monotonicity tests in both historical and simulated domains. Higher fragility regimes are systematically associated with greater conditional tail damage. Robustness checks across ensemble size, shock scaling, and fragility specification confirm the stability of scenario ordering and conditional risk gradients. An extended calibration exercise further indicates that, in HY spreads, model-implied fragility operates primarily as a short-horizon dynamic signal: differential specifications outperform static levels in out-of-sample forward conditioning tests. The contribution is methodological rather than predictive. The framework establishes a structured and internally reproducible pipeline for regime-sensitive risk analysis under controlled structural assumptions, consistent with a local phase-space interpretation of systemic vulnerability.

detail.abstract: Green Deals have been introduced across Western economies as large-scale, mission-oriented innovation policies (MOIPs) intended to combine economic growth with environmental sustainability. Rooted in the concept of an "entrepreneurial state," these initiatives reflect renewed confidence in governments' ability to direct technological and industrial transformation. However, their outcomes have frequently diverged from expectations. This volume examines the theoretical foundations and empirical results of Green Deals, highlighting the institutional, economic, and behavioral factors that contribute to their shortcomings. Drawing on perspectives from evolutionary economics, public choice theory, and behavioral political economy, the contributors analyze a wide range of cases, including Germany's Energiewende, Italy's Superbonus, and the European Union's hydrogen and battery programs. Across these examples, recurring challenges such as rent-seeking, mission capture, optimism bias, and distorted incentives are identified. The findings indicate that while Green Deals have advanced ambitious sustainability goals, they often undermine competitiveness and fiscal stability while generating limited environmental benefits. The volume concludes by outlining alternative pathways that emphasize incremental, technologyneutral, and institutionally grounded approaches to sustainability-approaches that align more closely with long-term economic resilience and effective environmental policy.

title: Closing Small Open Economy: Spectral Evidence on Domestic Business Cycles
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Closing Small Open Economy: Spectral Evidence on Domestic Business Cycles
detail.abstract: This paper identifies a dominant Main Business Cycle (MBC) shock in a small open economy and demonstrates its empirical relevance using frequency-based Max-Share identification. Analyzing quarterly Korean data (2000-2019), we show that the MBC shock drives synchronized short-run fluctuations in output, consumption, and investment, while a distinct long-run shock tied to total factor productivity (TFP) governs low-frequency dynamics. This temporal disconnect highlights the coexistence of demand-driven cycles and structural supply forces. Unlike in large economies, inflation reacts sharply and non-monotonically, supporting models with nonlinear, state-dependent pricing. Moreover, consumption responds more strongly than other real variables, and the trade balance moves countercyclically, underscoring the role of financial frictions. By isolating domestic cyclical dynamics from global drivers, this study illustrates how data-driven, frequency-domain methods can reveal propagation mechanisms overlooked in conventional frameworks, with implications for modeling and policy in open economies.

detail.abstract: Private information in financial markets enhances the informational content of asset prices and thereby supports efficient resource allocation. Yet, informed traders extract rents at the expense of uninformed traders, generating a tradeoff between price informativeness and liquidity costs. Moreover, equilibrium investment in information acquisition may be socially excessive or insufficient. We show that a market structure separating the market for information from the market for liquidity can simultaneously deliver price informativeness, preserve liquidity, and align private incentives with efficient levels of information production.

detail.title: Pitfalls and Optimal Design of Emergency Liquidity Assistance
detail.abstract: This paper studies why lender-of-last-resort support can fail to stop bank runs. In a nominal bank-run model with equity and multiple banks, I show that delayed Emergency Liquidity Assistance (ELA) shifts losses onto patient depositors and can trigger panic-driven withdrawals, even with sound assets and unlimited centralbank liquidity. The mechanism is a crisis-contingent, economy-wide inflation tax that insures early withdrawals while taxing those who stay, and redistributes resources across banks through the price level. The results highlight that ELA timing and fiscal design are critical for stability and can make regulatory interventions destabilizing rather than stabilizing.

title: Enterprise Optimization Through Big Data Analytics: Operational Performance and Financial Outcomes in Fintech-Driven Acquisitions

detail.title: Enterprise Optimization Through Big Data Analytics: Operational Performance and Financial Outcomes in Fintech-Driven Acquisitions
detail.abstract: This paper examines how enterprise optimization enabled by data and analytics capabilities translates into operational performance and financial outcomes in a large fintech-driven acquisition. Using London Stock Exchange Group's (LSEG) $27 billion acquisition of Refinitiv (completed January 2021) as a case study, we apply quantitative financial analysis over 2016-2025 to evaluate whether integrating a leading data-and-analytics business improved profitability, solvency, and competitive positioning. Results reveal a fundamental paradox: operational metrics improved substantially post-acquisition (EBITDA grew 4.2×, revenue expanded 4.4×), yet reported financial health weakened due to acquisition financing and accounting effects. LSEG's Altman Z-Score declined from 6.47 (safe zone, 2019) to 0.04 (distress zone, 2020), reaching 0.11 by 2024, reflecting leverage and the enlarged balance sheet. While integration delivered £854 million annual run-rate synergies, cumulative amortization charges (£4.0 billion) and interest expense (£2.8 billion) absorbed much of the operational gains. Peer benchmarking indicates 1 LSEG Refinitiv Acquisition Analysis 2 LSEG's profitability margins remained 30-40% below competitors. The findings show that enterprise optimization through big data analytics can succeed operationally, but value creation depends critically on financing structure and the translation of synergies into net earnings.

title: The Future Of Nigeria Trademarks Registration With Artificial Intelligence: A Money Bag For The Nigerian Economy

detail.title: The Future Of Nigeria Trademarks Registration With Artificial Intelligence: A Money Bag For The Nigerian Economy
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how businesses operate in Nigeria and across the globe. One of such areas experiencing this transformation is intellectual property (IP) law, particularly trademark registration. Trademarks are critical for branding and market differentiation, and Nigeria's economy stands to benefit greatly from more efficient trademark processes, especially in a digitising commercial environment. 1 In recent years, AI technologies have been applied to various stages of trademark managementfrom searching for existing marks to drafting applications and monitoring for infringements. 2 This article examines how AI is being integrated into Nigeria's trademark registration system, the benefits it offers, and the challenges that must be addressed. It also explores current government initiatives, real-world examples, and future projections for AI-driven trademarks in Nigeria, underscoring how this could become a "money bag" for the Nigerian economy by boosting innovation, investment, and brand protection.

title: Narrative Credibility and the Future of the U.S. Dollar: Governance, Confidence, and Monetary Power in a Fragmented World

detail.title: Narrative Credibility and the Future of the U.S. Dollar: Governance, Confidence, and Monetary Power in a Fragmented World
detail.abstract: This paper argues that reserve currencies fail politically before they fail mechanically. While prevailing accounts of de-dollarization emphasize technical substitution-such as alternative payment systems, reserve reallocation, or BRICS settlement mechanisms-this paper reframes reserve-currency stability as a problem of expectational governance. It introduces narrative credibility as an analytical category, defined as the perceived coherence and intelligibility of governance signals across fiscal policy, central bank independence, trade regimes, and alliance commitments. When these signals diverge, confidence can erode endogenously even as monetary dominance remains intact. Drawing on historical evidence from sterling's decline (1945-1972) and the contemporary U.S. context, the paper identifies a generalizable mechanism applicable to reservecurrency states operating under fiscal saturation and geopolitical fragmentation. To operationalize this mechanism, it proposes a Governance Legibility Index (GLI) that measures cross-domain institutional signaling coherence. Rather than predicting currency displacement or collapse, the framework explains how gradual signaling drift incrementally destabilizes monetary confidence, generating diversification and hedging behavior in the absence of a viable alternative reserve system.

title: Triangulus: Toward a Binary-Triangular Model of Contextual Computation An Intermediate Computational Architecture Between Binary and Quantum Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Triangulus: Toward a Binary-Triangular Model of Contextual Computation An Intermediate Computational Architecture Between Binary and Quantum Systems
detail.abstract: We propose Triangulus, a novel computational architecture that introduces triangular logic as a mediating layer between classical binary computation and quantum systems. Unlike binary logic, which operates on binary states (0/1, true/false), Triangulus introduces a third structural primitive: context. This framework addresses fundamental limitations in binary systems' ability to represent uncertainty, contradiction, perspective, and contextual validity. We demonstrate that Triangulus can be implemented on classical multi-core hardware without requiring quantum physical properties, while solving classes of problems that quantum computation cannot address. The architecture provides a computational grammar for arbitration, interpretation, and contextual resolution, positioning itself as both a precursor to and governor of quantum computational systems. We formalize the theoretical foundations, examine hardware implementations, and propose practical applications in artificial intelligence, decision systems, and human-computer interaction.

title: Optimistic Resolution Mechanisms for Prediction Markets: Incentives, Equilibria, and Design Limits
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Economics and Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Optimistic Resolution Mechanisms for Prediction Markets: Incentives, Equilibria, and Design Limits
detail.abstract: This paper studies the incentive fragility of the resolution layer adopted by major crypto prediction markets. We model settlement as a strategic game between a proposer and potential disputers who face costly verification. Disputers may free-ride, producing a nochallenge equilibrium in which incorrect reports finalize. Adjudication noise further weakens deterrence by lowering the expected return to disputing. We microfound adjudication as token-weighted voting and derive a concentration-sensitive Hoeffding bound that motivates an empirical Adjudication Risk Index (ARI). Using UMA voting and staking data from 2020-2026, we estimate daily voting correctness and construct event-level and daily ARIs, documenting pronounced time variation and spikes that coincide with periods of increased voting-power concentration.

title: Efficiency Dynamics of Indian Public Sector Banks postliberalisation: A DEA and Tobit Analysis (1991-2024)
affiliations: Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) - Department of Commerce, Aligarh Muslim University Aligarh and Aligarh Muslim University Aligarh

detail.title: Efficiency Dynamics of Indian Public Sector Banks postliberalisation: A DEA and Tobit Analysis (1991-2024)
detail.abstract: This study examines the operational efficiency and reform-induced performance dynamics of Indian public sector banks in the post-liberalisation era. We use Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) under Constant and Variable Returns to Scale to evaluate the trends in technical, pure technical, and scale efficiency over the period 1991-2024, with particular emphasis on the impact of large-scale bank mergers. A second-stage Tobit regression model is employed to identify the financial determinants influencing efficiency scores during 1996-2024. The results reveal persistent input-oriented inefficiencies in the pre-merger period, followed by a marked improvement in efficiency and convergence among banks after consolidation. Capital adequacy emerges as the most significant positive determinant of efficiency, highlighting the role of strong capitalisation in enhancing operational performance. In contrast, return on assets exhibits a statistically significant and negative association with efficiency, while bank size shows a negative but statistically insignificant relationship. The findings provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of banking reforms and consolidation policies in improving the efficiency of public sector banks in India, and offer policy-relevant insights for strengthening resilience, resource allocation, and long-term stability in the public banking system.

title: Microaggression Toward Filipino Women With Mobility Disabilities: From Microstories to Macrostruggles

detail.title: Microaggression Toward Filipino Women With Mobility Disabilities: From Microstories to Macrostruggles

declarations.funderStatement: We express our deepest appreciation to the University of the Philippines Center for Women’s and Gender Studies for funding our study through a grant.

detail.abstract: The Philippines has worked proactively to ensure equal rights and opportunities for persons with disabilities. Despite these efforts, the promise of disability-responsive and gender-transformative reforms has yet to be achieved. In particular, women with disabilities continue to face distinct forms of discrimination, such as microaggressions, which are often subtle yet common and are marginally covered by existing policies in the country. Guided by Keller and Galgay's (2010) domains of microaggressions and Ancha's (2022) experiences of microaggressions among women with disabilities in the Philippines, the present study employs convergent parallel mixed-method design to examine the experiences of microaggression among with with mobility disabilities in Tahanang Walang Hagdanan, Inc. Our study found that participants had limited awareness of the concept but affirmed that they had experienced different forms of microaggressions. Additionally, participants reported experiencing specific forms of microaggressions more frequently than others, leading to varying levels of discomfort and distress. Our study recommends integrating microaggression in the definitions of discrimination, increasing awareness of the concepts within gender and disability inclusion initiatives of organizations, and expanding literature on gender and disability research.

title: Asset Dynamics and Dissipative Structures in Open Economies: Economics as a Prescription for the "Thermal Death" of Equilibrium
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Asset Dynamics and Dissipative Structures in Open Economies: Economics as a Prescription for the "Thermal Death" of Equilibrium

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest associated with this manuscript.

detail.abstract:
This paper deepens the "Equilibrium Theory Endogenizing Imbalances" based on asset dynamics, as presented in the previous study (Kitamura, 2025), by incorporating concepts from thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. The objective is to bridge to a qualitative theory of development, encompassing issues such as the sustainability of economic growth and the creation of innovation. While the previous work proposed a model where imbalances are perpetuated through asset preference and capital diffusion, this study extends the framework into a model where "effective asset potential"—defined as the asset level divided by the rate of return on assets—acts as the driving force behind capital flows. It demonstrates a mechanism in which the capital efficiency of each nation significantly determines its economic trajectory.
Consequently, this paper reveals that individual economies exist under a tension between "subjective equilibrium" aimed at utility maximization, and the "pressure of entropy increase" inherent in asset dynamics. Through observations using multilateral data, the global economy has polarized into "self-organizing economies" that concentrate and accumulate capital, and "diffusive economies" that primarily disperse and dissipate capital. This paper presents a novel perspective that views the global economy as a "dissipative structure" maintained through the interdependence of these distinct phases.
Based on this analysis, the paper argues that for an economic system to remain sustainable, it is essential to maintain the gradient of asset potential within the system properly by eliminating "stagnation" through innovation and redistribution policies. Ultimately, this paper proposes that what economics terms "equilibrium" is equivalent to "thermal death" in physics; therefore, the goal of economics should be the avoidance rather than the realization of such a state, making the perspective of "entropy management".

title: CHANFORMER: An Encoder-Only Channel-Wise Transformer for Long-Term Multi-Asset Financial Time Series Forecasting
affiliations: Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics and Finance, , Lecturer, Ton Duc Thang University, FPT University, FPT University, FPT University and FPT University

detail.title: CHANFORMER: An Encoder-Only Channel-Wise Transformer for Long-Term Multi-Asset Financial Time Series Forecasting
detail.abstract: Forecasting financial price series encounters significant obstacles due to intense volatility, sudden changes in distributions, and intricate inter-asset correlations that vary with market conditions, which intra-sample multivariate approaches cannot properly handle. This study introduces CHANFORMER, a novel encoder-only channel-oriented Transformer designed for long-term prediction over closely linked cryptocurrencies and stocks. Through incorporating reversible instance normalization to address the previous bottlenecks, CHANFORMER compresses each channel's full input history into one high-dimensional token via projection, utilizes a standard Transformer encoder for pure cross-channel self-attention to capture interdependencies, and incorporates a dedicated channel-mixing multi-layer perceptron to enable dynamic nonlinear fusion across assets. CHANFORMER concurrently produces predictions for 50 OHLCV channels per cryptocurrency and stock group. Empirically, CHANFORMER surpasses state-ofthe-art Transformers with average error decreases of 29% relative to closest rivals and 83-94% against classical variants. Throughout backtesting strategies, the long-short approach delivers robust positive total returns of 59% in crypto with Sharpe 1.09 over 364 days, and the architecture ensures operational viability with approximately 23 minutes of training along with 1.6 seconds inference time at a total of 0.107 kWh and 0.051 kg CO 2 computation overhead. Therefore, this advances channel-centric designs for high-dimensional multi-asset analysis in financial sequence prediction.

title: The Evolution of Corporate Social Responsibility and Its Impact on Financial Success

detail.title: The Evolution of Corporate Social Responsibility and Its Impact on Financial Success
detail.abstract: This article examines the evolution of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and its relationship to long-term financial performance. Tracing CSR from its philanthropic origins, the paper synthesizes contemporary literature on governance, sustainability, and corporate strategy. It argues that CSR has transitioned from a peripheral moral obligation to a mechanism that enhances firm value. Particular attention is given to the integration of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) initiatives as a modern implementation of CSR. The paper also evaluates emerging regulatory and technological developments that are likely to shape the future trajectory of CSR. While acknowledging criticisms and measurement challenges, the analysis concludes that firms embedding CSR into core strategic operations are better positioned to achieve sustainable competitive advantage.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between Pan-Africanism and democratic movements, highlighting how Pan-Africanism is increasingly integrated into the latter. It employs a structured methodology, analysing qualitative data from various online literature and expert insights. They meticulously selected 34 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 1947 to 2026, each discussing the reasons that led Pan-Africanism to be swallowed by democracy. The data highlights the limitations of uncertainty in governing institutions in African countries, emphasizing the influence of democratic ideals on Pan-Africanism. The movement, advocating for unity and empowerment among African peoples, faces challenges such as the institutionalization of democracy leveraging Pan-Africanist rhetoric for political legitimacy, a focus on national identities over continental unity, and fragmentation due to regional conflicts.

Moreover, the article explores how adopting democratic frameworks has sometimes weakened Pan-African principles as political leaders focus on individual state governance, neglecting broader continental goals. This study reveals a paradox where the pursuit of democratic governance, seen as a means of liberation, may unintentionally diminish the solidarity vital to Pan-Africanism. By synthesising existing literature, it offers insights into the interaction between democracy and Pan-Africanism, aiming to identify ways to reintegrate Pan-Africanism into modern democratic discussions for an agenda that aligns with the original aspirations of the movement.

title: The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and Michigan State University - Eli Broad College of Business

detail.title: The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fisher College of Business Working Paper No. 2026-03-002
publicationDetails.journalName: Ohio State University, Fisher College of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: There are three classic problems in corporate finance: capital structure, real investment, and payout policy. In three companion papers, we characterize the max EPS solution to each one. The max EPS approach delivers an optimal leverage ratio even in the absence of frictions, an investment rule based on comparing yields rather than using a risk-adjusted discount rate, and a payout policy where accretive buybacks are preferred to neutral dividends. Our max EPS model draws a bright line between growth and value.  Growth stocks have earnings yields below the riskfree rate; value stocks have earnings yields above it. This single comparison leads the two kinds of firms to pursue different constellations of EPS-maximizing policies. The model also produces   easy-to-follow calculations that closely mirror what practitioners actually do. This review article ties together these results to form a new max EPS paradigm for corporate-finance research.

title: The Role of Visual Communication in the Impact of Transformational Leadership on Organizational Development in a Few Chosen Ghanaian Organizations
affiliations: NATIONAL ELECTRONIC MEDIA INSTITUTE OF SOUTH AFRICA and

detail.title: The Role of Visual Communication in the Impact of Transformational Leadership on Organizational Development in a Few Chosen Ghanaian Organizations
detail.abstract: Purpose: The study's specific goals were to evaluate the following: 1) the effect of transformational leadership on organizational development; 2) the effect of visual communication on organizational development; and 3) the moderating effect of visual communication on the relationship between transformational leadership and organizational development. Design/Methodology: A review of pertinent literature on the study constructs was conducted. The underlying idea of the hypothesis development was the leadermember exchange (LMX) theory. Because the study used a quantitative research methodology, questionnaires were the primary tool used to collect data for the study. Additionally, the study used explanatory and descriptive research purposes. Using the SPSS PROCESS macro model 4, 400 respondents from selected organisations in Ghana's Ashanti Region provided data for the study. Findings: The results of the study (B.2377, P=<.05) indicate that transformational leadership positively and significantly predicts organizational development. Again, the study's analysis (B=.0518, P=<.05) shows that visual communication positively and significantly predicts organizational development. Finally, the results of the study (B=.0178, P=<.05) show that visual communication has a positive and significant moderation on the relationship between transformational leadership and organizational development. Practical Implications: The study suggested that to help organisations in Ghana develop their organisational development, transformational leadership, and visual communication capabilities to be efficient and effective as business organisations, policy and legislative makers, such as the Ministry of Trade and Industry, should organise training workshops and programmes. Originality: This study offers a novel empirical exploration of the mutually reinforcing relationship between organizational development and transformational leadership in a subset of Ghanaian organisations. By recognizing visual communication as a crucial, hitherto unexplored moderating factor that enhances the effectiveness of visionary leadership in promoting institutional growth, it sets a new standard.

title: Feature Comment: Twenty-Five Cent AI: The Hidden Costs of Promotional AI Deals
affiliations: George Washington University - Law School

detail.abstract: The General Services Administration’s OneGov initiative offers federal agencies access to leading AI platforms—including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Copilot, and Perplexity—at promotional prices ranging from free to one dollar per agency. This Feature Comment examines how these nominal price points function as the procurement equivalent of loss-leader pricing: low enough to accelerate adoption while obscuring lifecycle costs, operational dependency, and diminished negotiating leverage at renewal. Drawing on the Federal Acquisition Regulation’s buying-in framework (FAR 3.501), switching-cost theory, and publicly available reseller pricing data, the Comment demonstrates that the gap between promotional and post-promotional pricing can be substantial—and that most renewal terms are not publicly disclosed. It analyzes how behavioral and organizational lock-in develops during promotional periods through workflow integration, institutional habit formation, and the erosion of in-house capacity, and explains why exit rights not secured before adoption are difficult to negotiate afterward. The Comment identifies transparency and governance gaps in the current OneGov structure and proposes a risk mitigation framework organized at the contract, operational, and program levels—including binding post-promotional pricing, structured pilot constraints, dependency tracking, and uniform public disclosure of lifecycle terms as a condition of OneGov participation.

title: Compound Markups: A Theory of Price Amplification in Production Networks

detail.title: Compound Markups: A Theory of Price Amplification in Production Networks
detail.abstract: This paper introduces compound markups in production networks: the wedge between observed prices and the pure-cost prices that would prevail if all output markups were set to one, holding technology and primary-factor prices fixed. The main contribution is a representation theorem showing that, in a Cobb-Douglas network, compound markups are obtained by applying the Leontief inverse of the intermediate-share matrix to any vector of direct markups measured at market input prices. The paper provides a walk decomposition for upstream attribution, a strongly connected component decomposition that isolates feedback loops, and bounds on amplification and truncation error. Extensions relate the approach to the classic input-output price model and to local results for general unit-cost functions. A short illustration shows how loops raise price-to-resource-cost wedges. The framework enables IO-implementable attribution of final-price wedges to upstream market power and supports applications to cost-of-living measurement, inflation pass-through, and policy incidence.

title: Mergers and Non-contractible Benefits: The Employees' Perspective
affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University in the City of New York and Columbia University

detail.title: Mergers and Non-contractible Benefits: The Employees' Perspective
detail.abstract:
Incomplete contract theory, supported by anecdotal evidence, suggests that when a firm is acquired, workers may be adversely affected in non-contractible aspects of their work experience. This paper empirically investigates this prediction by combining M\&A events from the Refinitiv database and web-scraped Glassdoor review data. We find that: (a) Controlling for pre-trends, mergers lead to lower satisfaction, especially on non-contractible dimensions of the employee experience (about 6% of a standard deviation); (b) The effect is stronger in the target firm than in the acquiring firm; (c) Text analysis of employee comments indicates that the decline in satisfaction is primarily associated with perceived breaches of implicit contracts. Our findings indicate that mergers may reduce workers' job utility through non-monetary channels.
