title: Mapping policy priorities and family needs in regional official documents of Northeast Italy using generative text analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University College Dublin (UCD), University of Padua, University of Ferrara and University of Padua

detail.title: Mapping policy priorities and family needs in regional official documents of Northeast Italy using generative text analysis
detail.abstract: Family well-being is a cornerstone of social and economic stability, influencing both individual development and broader societal dynamics. Recently, declining birth rates, population aging, and economic instability have significantly reshaped family structures in Italy. Regional administrations, particularly in Northeast Italy (Friuli Venezia Giulia, Trentino-Alto Adige, Veneto, and Emilia-Romagna), hold considerable autonomy in family policy development. However, the extent to which these policies align with actual family needs remains unclear. This study evaluates whether regional policies reflect principles of anticipatory governance, which emphasize proactive, adaptive approaches to emerging societal challenges. Specifically, the paper aims to identify family-related policies and needs articulated in official documents from 2018 to 2022 and assess the alignment and potential gaps between them. We applied generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs), to analyze unstructured legislative texts retrieved from official regional websites. The method integrated topic modeling, structured policy, and needed extraction using tailored prompts, and inter-regional comparisons via the Jaccard similarity metric. Findings reveal diverse regional priorities but common challenges, including mental health support, childcare accessibility, economic vulnerability, and fragmented service delivery. This study demonstrates the value of GPT-based text analysis in assessing policy effectiveness, enhancing the responsiveness and inclusivity of family-oriented policies in a rapidly changing social landscape.

title: Analysis of Italian Electricity Prices

detail.title: Analysis of Italian Electricity Prices
detail.abstract: The Italian average daily price of electricity is analysed, in order to price different types of derivatives. The analysis starts with an overview of the legal and operational setting of the Italian electricity market at large. Then, the time series of daily average prices is manipulated, so that seasonal components are removed. The stochastic componentsis afterwards tested with several techniques with the aim of investigating its supposed mean reverting behaviour. The last part of the work deals with setting up a model, capable of effectively predicting prices. The model takes into account the mean reverting and spiky nature of prices. The market price of risk is retrieved from pricesof futures, available on the market. The fully calibrated model offers a predicted price, which is used as strike price for the evaluation of European, American and Bermudan call and put options.

title: Optimal Econometric Models for Forecasting Peru's National Income
affiliations: Universidad Nacional de Frontera, Universidad Nacional de Frontera and Universidad Nacional de Frontera

detail.title: Optimal Econometric Models for Forecasting Peru's National Income
detail.abstract: The objective of this research was to estimate an optimal econometric model for the forecast of Peru's National Income, using the Box-Jenkins methodology applied to quarterly time series corresponding to the period 2000-2021. The study adopted a quantitative, applied-type approach, with an observational and longitudinal design, using data from the Central Reserve Bank of Peru and the Ministry of Economy and Finance. The sample was made up of 88 quarterly observations of National Income, expressed in percentage variation. In the identification stage, the graphical analysis showed an increasing long-term trend and non-constant variability in the series. Likewise, the correlogram showed significant self-correlations in more than 33 lags, which indicated temporal dependence in the series. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit root test (ADF) confirmed the non-stationarity of the National Income in levels, obtaining a t-statistic of-2.793668, a value lower in absolute terms than the critical values at 1%, 5% and 10%, which implies the presence of a unit root and the need to differentiate the series to achieve stationarity. Subsequently, the Box-Jenkins methodology was applied for the estimation of econometric models, evaluating their predictive capacity through the analysis of prognostic errors and diagnostic criteria. The results showed that National Income shows a sustained upward trend during the period analyzed, reflecting the dynamic behavior of Peru's economic growth. Likewise, the estimated econometric models proved to be adequate tools for forecasting, allowing to capture the temporal structure of the series and generate reliable estimates for future periods. In conclusion, the Box-Jenkins methodology is an effective econometric instrument for the modeling and forecasting of Peru's National Income, contributing to economic policy decision-making by generating projections based on empirical and statistical evidence.

title: Financial Development And Economic Growth In Nigeria: Asymmetric Cointegration And Threshold Analysis
affiliations: Caleb University

detail.title: Financial Development And Economic Growth In Nigeria: Asymmetric Cointegration And Threshold Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the nonlinear relationship between financial development and economic growth in Nigeria, covering the period from 1980 to 2018, in an effort to explain the direction of linearities and determine the exact threshold policy points for financial development variables. The financial development proxies adopted in the study are broad money and credit to the private sector. While deploying the nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) approach to ascertain the asymmetric cointegration status of financial development and GDP growth, the turning point between the variables of study is estimated using the threshold regression approach. The findings from the NARDL analysis show that the relationship between the financial development variables and economic growth are cointegrated in the long run and have a U-shaped asymmetrical relationship. Furthermore, the discrete threshold regression analysis reveals that while the switching point for broad money is 17.73% of GDP, it is 6.03% of GDP for credit to the private sector. Therefore, whenever the level of the financial development indicators falls below the estimated tipping point, there is a drag on the country's economic growth. The study recommends the implementation of the financial development threshold points as the minimum levels by which to achieve positive effects on the country's economic growth. A further recommendation to achieve rapid progress in financial development entails the rapid monetisation of financial transactions and the expansion of financial access as well as the strengthening of efficiency and regulation of the financial markets.

title: Dynamic Adverse Selection with Flow Limited Liability: A Closed-Form Approach to Price Regulation
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice - Dipartimento di Economia and University of Padua, Dep of Economics and Management

detail.title: Dynamic Adverse Selection with Flow Limited Liability: A Closed-Form Approach to Price Regulation
detail.abstract: This paper studies a continuous-time regulatory problem in which a firm holds persistent private information about demand and is subject to a flow limited-liability constraint. The regulator regulates prices through a dynamic mechanism that ensures truthful reporting of the evolving type. Limited liability imposes a state-dependent lower bound on the firm's instantaneous utility, inducing a reflecting boundary in continuation utility and giving rise to a tractable singular-control representation. We derive closed-form expressions for the optimal pricing rule and the associated continuation-utility function, and we characterize the optimal up-front transfer required to induce truthful revelation of the firm's initial type. The resulting contract is fully explicit and highlights how limited liability shapes information rents and regulatory distortions over time.

title: The Adaptive Environmental Capacity Theory (AECT)

detail.title: The Adaptive Environmental Capacity Theory (AECT)
detail.abstract:
Conventional environmental governance frameworks largely treat nature either as a passive resource base or as an externality correctable through market pricing mechanisms. Such approaches rely on implicit assumptions of marginal damage, proportional system response, and reversibility—assumptions increasingly contradicted by empirical evidence of non-linear ecological stress accumulation, delayed collapse, and irreversible threshold breaches.

This paper introduces the Adaptive Environmental Capacity Theory (AECT), a systems-based environmental governance framework that conceptualizes the environment as a finite, heterogeneous, and regenerative capacity system constrained by biological regeneration rates and critical thresholds. Rather than proposing a single optimization equation, AECT formalizes a Capacity–Load–Regeneration–Threshold (CLRT) structure and an adaptive decision rule that governs economic and institutional activity within ecological safety limits.

AECT reframes sustainability from an efficiency and pricing problem into a continuous capacity management challenge, emphasizing precautionary buffers, threshold respect, and regeneration prioritization. The framework explicitly rejects marginal optimization beyond ecological safety boundaries and argues that certain losses cannot be compensated through financial mechanisms once thresholds are crossed.

By integrating ecological limits directly into governance logic rather than post-damage correction tools, AECT offers a policy-relevant, institution-compatible foundation for managing environmental stability across production, service, and urban systems. The theory is presented as a conceptual governance framework that invites future empirical calibration and subsystem-specific operationalization.

title: The Systematic Omission Of Economic Education In Colombia: An Institutional Analysis And A Pedagogical Solution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Systematic Omission Of Economic Education In Colombia: An Institutional Analysis And A Pedagogical Solution
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the institutional mechanisms that have systematically excluded economic education from Colombia's mandatory curriculum despite its critical importance for civic competence and economic development. Using institutional analysis and comparative education policy research, I demonstrate that the absence of economic education is not accidental but rather the result of converging incentives among educational institutions, policymakers, and social actors. I document the consequences through literacy data showing that only 43% of Colombians understand inflation and 48% of households are over-indebted. The paper proposes a pedagogical framework based on accessible language and practical application, demonstrated in The Truths Behind a Lie: The Government, the Economy, and Your Money, and presents actionable policy recommendations within Colombia's current legal framework. The findings have implications for education policy in Latin America and contribute to the literature on economic literacy and institutional design in educational systems.

title: Selective Inclusion and Colonial Institutions: Rethinking the Settler-Extractive Distinction in Long-Run Development
affiliations: Kajaani University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Selective Inclusion and Colonial Institutions: Rethinking the Settler-Extractive Distinction in Long-Run Development
detail.abstract: The institutional approach to development typically classifies colonial institutions as inclusive or extractive. This categorization is based on formal design. This classification often overlooks how rights and protections were distributed within societies, assuming access rather than measuring it. This paper develops a Selective Inclusion framework, arguing that colonial regimes frequently built formally capable institutions while restricting access for indigenous and majority populations. To operationalize this idea, I construct a Partial Access Index (PAI) measured at independence for a sample of 62 former colonies. The index codes access in four domains: political franchise, access to executive constraints, legal uniformity, and educational-economic participation. Descriptive evidence reveals a Settler Colony Paradox: countries commonly treated as benchmarks of inclusive institutions often exhibited substantial exclusion of non-settler populations. Empirically, higher institutional access is associated with lower long-term income inequality. Robustness checks, including jackknife and region-exclusion tests, confirm that this relationship is not driven by outliers. The pattern is non-linear and region-specific. title: The Labor Market Consequences of Rapid Sectoral Shifts
affiliations: Princeton University and Dartmouth College

detail.title: The Labor Market Consequences of Rapid Sectoral Shifts
detail.abstract:
Sectoral shifts require costly labor reallocation for workers, fueling concerns about how quickly they occur. We study how the pace of such sectoral shifts affects workers at risk of displacement. We develop a life-cycle model with skill heterogeneity and job ladders where labor demand gradually rises in one sector and declines in another. The model reveals three novel insights. First, workers’ lifetime earnings are strongly non-linear and even nonmonotonic in the horizon over which the transition unfolds. Second, more and more workers benefit on the extensive margin as the transition accelerates, but the tail of losses becomes thicker on the intensive margin. Third, labor market frictions are important to quantify these non-linearities. We apply our model to the climate transition and find substantial earnings losses from a transition ending in 2060. Completing the transition ten years earlier reduces average losses, but raises losses in the tail by a fifth.

title: The Market Value of Reproductive Rights: Evidence from U.S. Housing Markets
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Texas A&M University and The College of Wooster

detail.title: The Market Value of Reproductive Rights: Evidence from U.S. Housing Markets
detail.abstract:
We estimate the market value of reproductive rights as capitalized into U.S. housing markets. We do so using a synthetic difference-in-differences design to evaluate the effects of total abortion bans following the 2022 Dobbs decision, and drawing on housing market indices from Zillow and vacancy rate data from the U.S. Census Bureau's Housing Vacancy Survey. The results indicate that total abortion bans reduced rents by an average of 2.2% from July 2022 through June 2025, with the effect reaching 4.0% in the most recent year. Over the same horizon, bans increased rental vacancy rates by an average of 1.1 percentage points, with the effect reaching 1.8 percentage points in the most recent year. Estimates for home values and homeowner vacancy rates are similar in magnitude but less precise.

title: Why People Disagree About What Drives Stock Prices
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and Minneapolis Fed

detail.title: Why People Disagree About What Drives Stock Prices
detail.abstract:
We show that, to a first-order approximation, estimates of fluctuations in Shiller’s fundamental price relative to observed price depend primarily on forecasts of long-horizon expected returns. Researchers using different measures of cash flow and valuation may reach different conclusions about the extent to which values fluctuate excessively relative to fundamentals, but that is only because return forecasts based on different cash-flow-to-value measures will be different. Using U.S. equity data, we demonstrate that the amount of persistence in expected returns, rather than the amount of short-run return predictability, is the key determinant of implied excess volatility. Disagreements about stock market valuation therefore reduce to disagreements about long-run expected returns.

title: Pay Now, Buy Never: The Economics of Consumer Prepayment Schemes
affiliations: China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Pay Now, Buy Never: The Economics of Consumer Prepayment Schemes
detail.abstract:
Prepaid consumption is a common feature of modern consumer markets and is often presented as a mutually beneficial arrangement: consumers receive upfront discounts, and firms secure future sales. We analyze a large-scale Pay Now, Buy Later (PNBL) program in which consumers prepay for restaurant credit with bonuses, and spend the balance later. Using detailed transaction data from over 4 million consumers, we document widespread balance breakage: approximately 40% of prepaid value is never used. Because many consumers underutilize their balances, merchants recover significantly more than the bonus cost. The median firm earns roughly $5.5 in breakage profit for every $1 of bonus credit issued. While PNBL participation does lead to modest increases in consumer spending over time, firms gain substantially more from breakage than from any loyalty-driven revenue. These findings challenge the prevailing win–win narrative: PNBL schemes often result in a significant transfer from consumers to firms. We develop a stylized contract model to illustrate the misaligned incentives firms face, and show through counterfactual analysis that a simple escrow policy with an appropriately chosen deposit requirement can realign firm incentives and generate more consumer-serving outcomes.

title: How does AI Distribute the pie? Large Language Models and the Ultimatum Game
affiliations: Banco Central do Brasil and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: How does AI Distribute the pie? Large Language Models and the Ultimatum Game
detail.abstract:
As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly tasked with autonomous decision making, understanding their behavior in strategic settings is crucial. We investigate the choices of various LLMs in the Ultimatum Game, a setting where human behavior notably deviates from theoretical rationality. We conduct experiments varying the stake size and the nature of the opponent (Human vs. AI) across both Proposer and Responder roles. Three key results emerge. First, LLM behavior is heterogeneous but predictable when conditioning on stake size and player types. Second, while some models approximate the rational benchmark and others mimic human social preferences, a distinct “altruistic” mode emerges where LLMs propose hyper-fair distributions (greater than 50%). Third, LLM Proposers forgo a large share of total payoff, and an even larger share when the Responder is human. These findings highlight the need for careful testing before deploying AI agents in economic settings.

title: Repression
affiliations: Yale University and Northwestern University

detail.title: Repression
detail.abstract:
We develop a conceptual framework of political repression. To motivate why states repress, we introduce the notion of the political project. The proposed framework is used to interpret two known stylized facts: 1) repression is higher in autocracies; and 2) repression has declined since the 1990s. We discuss under-researched aspects of political repression such as migration restrictions, the targeting of repression, and backlash. We conclude by bringing attention to the two main challenges for research on repression: 1) conceptualizing whether a given episode of repression is successful, and 2) the inherent selection problem in empirical measures of repression.

title: Measuring Payroll Employment: A Note on the Current Employment Statistics

detail.abstract:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Employment Statistics (CES) is a high-quality, closely watched indicator of labor market health and the business cycle. Recent revisions to CES data have garnered significant attention. I provide a primer on CES methodology and analyze recent survey response and data revision patterns. CES revisions actually tend to be small, but they have increased in recent years. I discuss potential ideas for improving the CES including expanding the data sample with internal or external data, adjusting the estimates with benchmark data more often, and enhancing estimation of establishment birth and death.

title: The Effects of a Sudden Stop in Low-Skilled Immigration: Evidence from Korea’s Guest Worker Program
affiliations: Yonsei University, University of California, Davis - Department of Economics and Yonsei University

detail.title: The Effects of a Sudden Stop in Low-Skilled Immigration: Evidence from Korea’s Guest Worker Program
detail.abstract:
As workforces in high-income countries age and shrink, immigrants increasingly fill entry-level, low-skilled jobs. We examine what happens when this labor supply is abruptly reduced, exploiting South Korea’s sudden suspension of its low-skilled guest worker program following the 2020 COVID-19 border closure. Using policy-driven variation in firms’ pre-pandemic reliance on immigrant labor, we show that the collapse in inflows led to a significant increase in firm exit. Among surviving firms, greater pre-pandemic dependence on immigrant workers resulted in production disruptions and operational delays. Firms did not respond by expanding domestic hiring to replace missing guest workers. Instead, they adjusted by reallocating incumbent Korean employees toward lower-skilled tasks, contributing to occupational downgrading and significant wage declines. These findings suggest that low-skilled immigrant workers were not easily substitutable in the short run and that tighter immigration constraints can impose substantial adjustment costs on both firms and native workers.

title: The Micro-Geography of Persuasion: Randomized Peer Exposure and Legislative Outcomes
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: The Micro-Geography of Persuasion: Randomized Peer Exposure and Legislative Outcomes
detail.abstract:
We find that randomly assigned peers play a sizable and unique role in shaping political economy. Closely seated, and exogenously assigned, US Senate peers have a significant impact on Congressional voting, shifting votes by 11.9 percentage points (t=7.34). Physical distance is the largest and most consistent of any characteristic outside of party or state in impacting voting behavior. The distance effect is concentrated in the closest peers, existing for up to 19.6 feet on the Senate floor, then dissipating. Close peers additionally increase the probability of aisle-crossing (voting with the opposite party), with the aisle-crossing impact being roughly eight times larger on the final votes on bills. We then utilize a state-of-the-art AI-enhanced computer vision model based on real-time interactions using CSPAN video data at every 10-second interval amongst Congressional members. Using these observed interactions, we find that face-to-face interactions are associated with significant impacts on immediately pending votes. The interactions are largely driven by distance, with aisle-seated Senators from both parties being amongst the most likely to engage in face-to-face interactions across party lines. By conducting counterfactuals through randomized Senate seating, 59 consequential bills would have switched outcomes over our 30-year sample period.

title: Restoring Nature, Creating Wealth: Evidence from Rural Households in Africa
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, University of Navarra - Finance and Harvard Business School

detail.title: Restoring Nature, Creating Wealth: Evidence from Rural Households in Africa
detail.abstract:
Human-driven degradation of ecosystems threatens both global biodiversity and the livelihoods of communities that depend on natural systems for production and income. Yet empirical evidence on the economic returns to restoring nature remains scarce. We examine whether nature-enhancing interventions can generate measurable improvements in household wealth, in addition to environmental benefits. We study a large-scale agroecological intervention implemented by Trees for the Future (TREES) across farms in sub-Saharan Africa, combining detailed household surveys with high-resolution satellite imagery. We show that quasi-exogenous increases in natural capital lead to substantial gains in household wealth, proxied by livestock ownership, of about 75% by the third year of treatment. Each dollar invested in the intervention returns about $2.28 in direct wealth benefits for participating farmers, before accounting for positive health impacts and carbon sequestration. We further document dramatic increases in tree cover and crop diversity, significant improvements in food security and dietary diversity, and detectable enhancements in vegetation indices measured from space. Together, these results demonstrate that restoring natural capital generates both ecological and economic returns, offering a scalable pathway for nature-positive development in rural economies where biodiversity remains a critical productive asset.

title: When Do Financial Frictions Matter for Misallocation?
affiliations: University of Rochester - Department of Economics, University of Rochester - Department of Economics, University of Georgia - Terry College of Business - Department of Finance and University of Missouri at Columbia - Department of Economics

detail.title: When Do Financial Frictions Matter for Misallocation?
detail.abstract:
This paper reassesses the role of financial frictions in capital misallocation through a model disciplined by both firm-level borrowing costs and the average revenue product of capital (ARPK). Using Chinese manufacturing data, we document substantial dispersion in ARPK, alongside a strong positive relationship between ARPK and the borrowing costs firms face---patterns absent in U.S. data. We develop a heterogeneous-firm model with endogenous firm-specific borrowing costs and additional capital distortions modeled as exogenous wedges. In this model, eliminating financial frictions raises total factor productivity (TFP) by 25 percentage points. In contrast, without other capital distortions, removing financial frictions increases TFP by less than 2 percentage points. The stark difference arises from the interaction between financial frictions and permanent firm-level distortions, which generate endogenous financial heterogeneity and selection, making productive firms the most constrained. Our findings suggest that financial frictions can be highly distortionary when other sources of misallocation are present.

title: Competition in Health Insurance Markets

detail.title: Competition in Health Insurance Markets
detail.abstract:
The United States relies primarily on private health insurance markets, yet these markets are highly concentrated and becoming more so over time. We document concentration across commercial, Medicare Advantage, and Medicaid markets. We then examine how asymmetric information—particularly adverse selection—interacts with market power to shape premiums, plan design, and consumer welfare. Empirical evidence confirms that insurer consolidation raises premiums. We discuss how antitrust enforcement, risk adjustment, regulation, and informational interventions shape competition and consumer welfare in these markets.

title: From Complaint to Action: Technology-Enabled Quality Improvement from Consumer Reviews
affiliations: Peking University - School of Economics,  and Department of Economics

detail.title: From Complaint to Action: Technology-Enabled Quality Improvement from Consumer Reviews
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how adopting an automated review monitoring system (ARMS) allows restaurants to translate consumer feedback into operational quality improvements. ARMS provides automated alerts for negative reviews and facilitates back-end work ticket management, reducing the costs of identifying, prioritizing, and addressing issues revealed by customer feedback. Using restaurant-level data on ARMS adoption and consumer reviews, we find that adoption increases average star ratings, lowers the share of negative reviews, and raises the positivity of review text. These improvements are not driven by strategic manipulation; they are greater for restaurants with lower initial ratings and in dimensions previously flagged as poor by consumers, consistent with the ARMS enhancing restaurant response to negative reviews. We also show that ARMS adoption partially crowds out front-end managerial responses, indicating a substitution between operational remediation and public replies, with the effect strongest when staff take a reflective approach to negative reviews. Finally, adoption is associated with greater consumer engagement, reflected in longer and more detailed reviews. Overall, our results suggest that online review systems, when paired with operational technology, can drive substantive quality improvements beyond mere reputation management.

title: Alternatives to 911
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Alternatives to 911
detail.abstract:
Almost a quarter-billion calls are placed to 911 each year in the United States. A large share of them involve social problems, not crimes or emergencies---yet police are dispatched in response. This review traces how the 911 emergency system's institutional design shapes demand for police, who is excluded from or ill served by this system, and what alternatives exist, including nonemergency lines (with police response), government hotlines (211, 311, 988), civilian crisis teams, and community-based resources. Among the universe of municipal police departments with at least 100 sworn officers in 2020, covering 107 million US residents, police have absorbed broad social service functions, with the availability of formal alternatives restricted to the largest cities. The evidence suggests that the primacy of police reflects institutional reproduction more than public need. I propose priorities for future research.

title: Tariffs, Automation, and Business Dynamism
affiliations: École Nationale de la Statistique et de l'Analyse de l'Information (ENSAI), University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Economics and University of Lausanne

detail.title: Tariffs, Automation, and Business Dynamism
detail.abstract:
Can protectionism revive domestic production, slow automation, and help routine workers? We address this question in a dynamic open-economy model with heterogeneous firms, endogenous entry, and task-based production in which routine tasks can be performed by workers or robots. Import tariffs reallocate demand toward domestic goods, reshape markups and entry incentives, and generate fiscal revenues rebated to households. As a result, tariffs raise GDP and consumption measured at market prices and temporarily slow automation, even though intermediate output at factor prices and trade volumes decline. The gains are unevenly distributed: routine workers benefit robustly through transfers and reduced training, non-routine workers face opposing wage and rebate effects, and firm owners gain in aggregate as higher domestic demand and entry expand total profits despite lower per-firm values. Aggregate welfare gains hinge critically on key assumptions (automation, training, endogenous entry) and on how tariff revenues are rebated. In the baseline with uniform transfers, the welfare-maximizing tariff lies below the classical monopoly formula, while alternative rebate schemes can shift it substantially. Overall, the results caution against viewing tariffs as a simple tool for reindustrialization and highlight the role of technology adoption and fiscal incidence in evaluating protectionist policies.

title: When Teachers Break the Rules: Imitation, Reciprocity, and Community Structure in the Transmission of Ethical Behavior
affiliations: University of Warwick - Department of Economics and The Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: When Teachers Break the Rules: Imitation, Reciprocity, and Community Structure in the Transmission of Ethical Behavior
detail.abstract:
We study how teachers' rule violations in grading affect students' ethical behavior. Using administrative data from high-stakes exams, combining teacher-assigned internal scores with externally graded national exam scores, we track teacher grading violations and subsequent student cheating. We explore three potential mechanisms: imitation (learning that rules can be broken), positive reciprocity (responding favorably to favorable treatment), and negative reciprocity (retaliating against unfavorable treatment). Exploiting within-student variation in exposure to different teachers, we find students are significantly more likely to cheat when teachers break the rules to their detriment (systematically undergrading), consistent with both imitation and negative reciprocity. However, when teachers systematically overgrade, responses vary by community structure. In heterogeneous communities, overgrading increases student cheating, suggesting imitation dominates. In homogeneous communities, students respond by cheating less, consistent with positive reciprocity dominating. This pattern holds across multiple homogeneity measures, including surname concentration and residential clustering. Survey measures of mutual respect and support between students and teachers confirm this pattern.

title: Personnel is Policy: Delegation and Political Misalignment in the Rulemaking Process
affiliations: Stanford University, Bocconi University, Northwestern University - Department of Managerial Economics and Decision Sciences (MEDS), Northwestern University - Department of Managerial Economics and Decision Sciences (MEDS), King’s College London and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: Personnel is Policy: Delegation and Political Misalignment in the Rulemaking Process
detail.abstract:
We combine comprehensive data on the rulemaking activities of the U.S. federal government with individual-level personnel and voter registration records to study delegation and principal-agent frictions in the development of new regulations. We present three main results. First, even important pieces of new regulation are frequently delegated to career bureaucrats who are politically misaligned with the president. Second, rules that are overseen by misaligned regulators take systematically longer to complete, are more verbose, generate more negative feedback from the public, and are more likely to be challenged in court. Third, in assigning regulators to rules, agency leaders often face a sharp trade-off between political alignment and expertise. Agency frictions notwithstanding, they tend to resolve this trade-off in favor of expertise.

title: General Social Agents
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: General Social Agents
detail.abstract:
Useful social science theories predict behavior across settings. However, applying a theory to make predictions in new settings is challenging: rarely can it be done without ad hoc modifications to account for setting-specific factors. We argue that AI agents put in simulations of those novel settings offer an alternative for applying theory, requiring minimal or no modifications. We present an approach for building such "general" agents that use theory-grounded natural language instructions, existing empirical data, and knowledge acquired by the underlying AI during training. To demonstrate the approach in settings where no data from that data-generating process exists--as is often the case in applied prediction problems--we design a heterogeneous population of 883,320 novel games. AI agents are constructed using human data from a small set of conceptually related but structurally distinct "seed" games. In preregistered experiments, on average, agents predict initial human play in a random sample of 1,500 games from the population better than (i) a cognitive hierarchy model, (ii) game-theoretic equilibria, and (iii) out-of-the-box agents. For a small set of separate novel games, these simulations predict responses from a new sample of human subjects better even than the most plausibly relevant published human data.

title: Who Gets What in Education: Can School Matching Improve Student Achievement?
affiliations: Duke University - Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and University of Chicago

detail.title: Who Gets What in Education: Can School Matching Improve Student Achievement?
detail.abstract:
We examine two approaches to improving urban school systems: changing who gets to go to existing schools (reallocation) and restructuring school portfolios through closures and reconstitution (resource augmentation). Using data from New York City high schools, we estimate models of school effects allowing for both vertical school quality differences and horizontal student-specific match effects. While sophisticated reallocation policies that optimize student-school matches can generate modest educational gains, they are constrained by limited seats at highly effective schools. Simple resource-augmentation policies targeting replacement of low-performing schools achieve comparable improvements with less systemic disruption. Analysis of NYC's school closures reveals that basic graduation rate metrics effectively identify struggling schools, suggesting complex value-added models may be unnecessary for targeting closure decisions. Our findings indicate that capacity constraints, rather than poor school matching, primarily drive educational inequality.

title: The Skill Premium in Times of Rapid Technological Change
affiliations: Boston University, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and Yale University

detail.title: The Skill Premium in Times of Rapid Technological Change
detail.abstract:
This paper shows that the pace of technology creation is a key driver of the skill premium. It develops a model in which skilled workers have a comparative advantage in learning new technologies. As technologies age, they become standardized and accessible to other workers. The skill premium is determined by the interplay between the pace of technology creation and standardization. A rapid pace of technology creation leads to a sustained increase in the skill premium. We calibrate the model using novel text-based data on new technologies and their changing demand for skills as they age. These data show that new technologies are initially skill intensive but become less so as they age. The data also point to an increased pace of new technology creation starting in the 1970s and tapering off in the 2000s. In response to this rapid pace of technology creation, the model generates a 32 percent increase in the college premium, which begins to reverse in the 2010s. Our framework also explains why the college premium is higher in dense cities, why its increase was mainly urban, and why it rose first for young workers and later for older workers.

title: Humans and AI On the Future Ahead of Us
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Humans and AI On the Future Ahead of Us
detail.abstract:
The convergence of artificial intelligence and mass-produced robotics is eliminating human labour as the primary engine of economic value. This paper argues that this displacement is structural and irreversible, and that the appropriate response is not mitigation but redesign — of economic systems, governance architectures, and the social contract itself.

Drawing on thinkers from Keynes and Aristotle to Masuda, Harari, and Ishiguro, the paper develops a three-part proposal. First, a resource-based economy in which the Earth's materials are managed as a common inheritance, extracted by autonomous systems, and distributed for the benefit of all. Second, a governance model replacing executive state apparatus with a small, lottery-selected human Council charged with custodianship of civilisational values, operating in partnership with AI systems conceived as Extended Intelligence rather than autonomous authority. Third, a fiscal architecture replacing all existing taxes with a single transaction levy financing a universal base income.

The paper further argues that extraterrestrial resource extraction is a necessary long-term extension of this model, and that the central challenge of the post-labour world is not material — it is philosophical: how human beings construct meaning when necessity no longer structures their lives.

title: Common Knowledge? Gender Differences in IP Rights Awareness
affiliations: ,  and World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO)

detail.title: Common Knowledge? Gender Differences in IP Rights Awareness

publicationDetails.detailsText: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Economic Research Working Paper Series No. 100
publicationDetails.journalName: World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Economic Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines gender disparities in intellectual property (IP) awareness and participation, using the 2023 and 2025 waves of the WIPO Pulse Survey conducted among 58,135 individuals across seventy-four countries. Our findings reveal that copyrights are the most recognized IP forms globally, while patents, trademarks and geographical indications remain the least familiar. At the individual level, women demonstrate lower knowledge of patents and trademarks, but greater knowledge of designs and copyrights compared to men, with these differences persisting after controlling for socioeconomic factors. These patterns are consistent with gendered specialization in education, professional and household spheres where women tend to cluster in creative industries while men dominate entrepreneurship and technical sectors. Notably, we observe a cohort effect: while we identify significant differences in knowledge between men and women for older cohorts, these disappear among younger cohorts. We do not observe comparable changes by level of education or occupation of respondents. Moreover, women exhibit more positive attitudes towards IP-protected products across categories. These findings highlight the need for targeted awareness campaigns and reveal that gendered patterns of IP knowledge may contribute to innovation gender gaps through educational pathways and professional specialization.

detail.abstract: A systemic risk has entered the financial sector's AI infrastructure that no existing supervisory instrument is designed to detect. As multinational banks deploy GenAI credit-scoring systems classified "High-Risk" under EU AI Act Annex III, they are building on data architectures inherited from legacy systems designed around formal, Western-centric financial identity. The populations invisible to those legacy systems remain invisible to the AI systems built on top of them. Denial decisions accumulate as training data. Each model generation encodes the previous generation's exclusions more deeply. The misconfiguration compounds-not within one institution, but across the industry-and will materialise as correlated capital shortfalls when market stress disproportionately affects the informal economies these models were never configured to see. This is not a compliance problem that one bank can solve by acting alone. It is a market failure requiring a regulatory instrument. This paper looks into that.

title: Admission Policies with Exam Retakes: Efficiency-Equity Trade-offs in Multidimensional Scoring
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Department of Information Systems & Operations Management

detail.title: Admission Policies with Exam Retakes: Efficiency-Equity Trade-offs in Multidimensional Scoring
detail.abstract: Admission systems worldwide increasingly allow students to take standardized entrance exams multiple times, yet institutions differ sharply in how they aggregate scores across attempts. These retake and aggregation policies shape students' incentives, influence who chooses to retake, and ultimately affect both the efficiency and equity of admissions. Using administrative data from the Chilean centralized admissions system, we document substantial heterogeneity in retaking behavior across socioeconomic groups and show that retaking is strongly associated with improved admission outcomes. Motivated by these patterns, we develop a stylized model in which students receive noisy math and verbal scores, a subset of students can retake the exam, and a single school admits applicants based on an application score derived from these components. We characterize equilibrium retaking behavior and admission cutoffs under four commonly used policies: first-attempt, last-attempt, best-attempt, and superscoring. The analysis reveals that last-attempt and best-attempt rules are equivalent, while superscoring can simultaneously reduce the average quality of admitted students and exacerbate socioeconomic disparities. A comprehensive simulation study shows that these conclusions are robust across a wide range of environments and are particularly sensitive to the cost of retaking and the informativeness of test scores. Taken together, our results highlight the central role of retake policies in shaping both efficiency and equity in competitive admissions and provide guidance for policymakers seeking to balance these objectives.

title: India's January 2026 CPI Inflation Under the Revised 2024 Base Year: Composition Effects and Underlying Price Pressures
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: India's January 2026 CPI Inflation Under the Revised 2024 Base Year: Composition Effects and Underlying Price Pressures
detail.abstract: India's January 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the first inflation reading under the revised 2024 base year series. Headline inflation was recorded at 2.75 percent, which is within the Reserve Bank of India's target band of 2 to 6 percent. While the aggregate result suggests that price pressures are restrained, a breakdown of the inflation print reveals significant compositional changes. Sharp price rises in precious metals, particularly silver and gold jewellery, contributed nearly 29 percent to the headline inflation rate. Excluding these volatile components reduces inflation to around 1.96 percent, bringing the underlying rate below the lower bound of the RBI's target range. The concentration of pricing pressures on a small number of commodity-linked items suggests that inflation remains relatively restricted and unevenly dispersed across the consumption basket. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing between transient commodity shocks and broad-based demand-driven inflation when assessing macroeconomic conditions and the monetary policy outlook.

title: The Impact of Close Corporations on Africa's Economic Landscape
affiliations: Durban University of Technology and Durban University of Technology

detail.title: The Impact of Close Corporations on Africa's Economic Landscape

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of close corporations on Africa's economic landscape, drawing insights from 24 scholarly articles that explore various dimensions of this phenomenon. Close corporations, characterised by limited shareholder numbers and closely held management, play a vital role in fostering entrepreneurship, creating jobs, and generating economic growth across the continent. Researchers adopted a structured approach, gathering and analysing qualitative data from a wealth of online literature sources and expert opinions. They meticulously selected 24 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 1984 to 2021, each discussing the Impact of Close Corporations on Africa's Economic Landscape. The data revealed the limitations of the growth of uncertainty to govern the Close Corporations on Africa's Economic Landscape. The systematic approach ultimately provided valuable insights into the struggles and challenges faced by Africans to manage the Close Corporations on Africa's Economic Landscape. The analysis reveals that these entities contribute significantly to local economies, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, retail, and informal markets. However, the paper also highlights the challenges they face, including regulatory hurdles, limited access to financing, and the need for greater transparency and governance. The research identifies key implications for policymakers, emphasising the importance of developing supportive frameworks that encourage the growth and sustainability of close corporations. It advocates for initiatives aimed at facilitating access to capital, enhancing regulatory environments, and promoting entrepreneurship education. Moreover, the study underscores the potential of close corporations to drive innovation and community development, especially in rural areas where opportunities are often scarce. In conclusion, while close corporations represent a formidable force in Africa's economic ecosystem, their full potential is hindered by systemic challenges. Addressing these issues is crucial for maximising their impact and ensuring that they contribute to broader economic development goals. This paper serves as a comprehensive resource for stakeholders interested in understanding the multifaceted role of close corporations in shaping Africa's economic future.

title: Assessing MSME Market Dynamics and Resilience in Phnom Penh: Challenges and Opportunities
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Cambodia Development Resource Institute (CDRI), Cambodia Development Resource Institute (CDRI), Cambodia Development Resource Institute (CDRI) and Cambodia Development Resource Institute (CDRI)

detail.title: Assessing MSME Market Dynamics and Resilience in Phnom Penh: Challenges and Opportunities
detail.abstract: This report examines the market dynamics and resilience of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Khan Meanchey, Phnom Penh, based on data from 14,820 establishments. MSMEs are deeply embedded in the urban economy, with nearly every household engaged in business activity. Despite a strong post-pandemic recovery in 2023, early signs of slowdown emerged in 2024 due to inflation, digital disruption, and rent insecurity. The high business turnover—1,790 openings versus 825 closures—reflects a survivalist approach to entrepreneurship rather than scalable growth. Most MSMEs remain informal and micro-scale, which limits their access to credit and formal support. Sectoral analysis reveals a concentration in low-productivity sectors, such as retail and food services, characterised by gender disparities and limited digital adoption. Formalisation and digital tools are linked to improved outcomes, especially in retail and hospitality. Manufacturing remains marginal and informal. Spatial analysis reveals localised resilience but highlights vulnerability to fluctuations in consumer demand, financial constraints, and tenancy issues. The report recommends targeted policy interventions, including formalisation incentives, digital transformation support, and inclusive training for women-led businesses. Strengthening MSME data systems and enabling secure access to tenancy and credit are essential for long-term resilience and inclusive urban development.

title: Informal Care & Mental Health: A Story of Unobserved Heterogeneity
affiliations: and Irdes - Institut de recherche et documentation en économie de la santé

detail.title: Informal Care & Mental Health: A Story of Unobserved Heterogeneity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by a grant from the French government, administered by the French National Research Agency (ANR) under the France 2030 program (grant reference ANR-22-PESN-0004), and is part of the activities of the Institute for Digital Health in Society (ISNS).

detail.abstract: In most European countries, long-term care systems rely heavily and increasingly on informal care provided by relatives. This work revisits the effect of informal care provision to old-age parents on the mental health of adults aged 50 to 75 using data from the Survey of Health, Aging and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). We apply the marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework, which enables the effect of informal care to be heterogeneous according to both observable and unobservable characteristics. We find a positive average treatment effect of informal care provision on the probability of being depressed, greater than that already estimated in the literature, which could lead to estimates of the cost of informal care being revised upwards. In addition, on average, informal care has a moderate effect (resp. has a large detrimental effect) on the mental health of individuals with a low (resp. large) unobserved resistance to care provision. Hence, compelling children who would not voluntarily choose to become caregivers to provide care may have deleterious consequences. With respect to observed characteristics, the detrimental effect on caregivers' mental health is lower for women and older individuals and is stronger for those living further from their parents. We do not find significant country differences.

title: The Extended Holiday Effect on the returns of Nikkei 225
affiliations: Independent and Independent

detail.title: The Extended Holiday Effect on the returns of Nikkei 225

keywords: Extended Forms of the Calendar Anomalies

detail.abstract: The best known form of the Holiday Effect refers to abnormal stock returns on a trading day before a public holiday and a trading day after. However, some investigations identified the Extended Holiday Effect, a form of seasonality that consists in abnormal stock returns occurring more than one trading day before or after a public holiday. This paper explores the presence of the Extended Holiday Effect on the returns of the Nikkei 225 index for two periods: 2009-2015 and 2016-2025. For the first period we identified abnormal high returns on three trading days before public holidays. In case of the second period we found abnormal high returns on two trading days after public holidays.

title: Child Marriage and Girls’ Secondary Education: Evidence from Fixed-Effects Panel Data
affiliations: West Windsor-Plainsboro High School North

detail.title: Child Marriage and Girls’ Secondary Education: Evidence from Fixed-Effects Panel Data
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between child marriage and female secondary education across countries from 2000 to 2023. Using publicly available data from UNICEF, UNESCO, and the Child Marriage Data Portal, I analyzed country-level indicators including child marriage prevalence (% of women aged 20–24 married before 18), female secondary school completion, GDP per capita, and urbanization. Preliminary analyses show that higher rates of child marriage are associated with lower female secondary enrollment and completion, a relationship that persists even after controlling for economic and urbanization factors. Comparisons between early (2000) and late (2022) years suggest that the negative association remains relatively stable over time, with slight variations across regions. Regression results indicate that a one-percentage-point increase in child marriage corresponds to approximately a -1.17 percentage point change in female secondary completion, holding GDP and urbanization constant.  These findings underscore the importance of addressing child marriage as a barrier to female education and highlight policy implications for governments and NGOs working to improve educational access for girls. The study contributes to the broader understanding of how social and economic factors interact to influence educational outcomes for young women globally.

title: Financial Well-Being
affiliations: University of Skovde - School of Business

detail.title: Financial Well-Being
detail.abstract: This chapter views financial wellbeing as a multidimensional concept that combines objective financial conditions, such as income and savings, with subjective perceptions of security, control, and satisfaction. It explains how financial literacy, financial capability, and financial self-efficacy contribute to responsible financial behavior, improved decision making, and long-term financial resilience. The chapter also analyzes financial stress as a key barrier to wellbeing, outlining its effects on cognition, mental health, work performance, and relationships. In addition, the discussion highlights the influence of demographic factors, socioeconomic status, and cultural norms on financial outcomes and perceptions. By integrating theoretical perspectives and empirical evidence from past researches, the chapter provides students with a clear framework for understanding how psychological, behavioral, structural, and cultural factors interact to shape financial wellbeing, offering insights relevant for research, policy, and practice.

title: When Machines Think for Us: Hannah Arendt, Agentic AI, and the Quiet Collapse of Judgment

detail.title: When Machines Think for Us: Hannah Arendt, Agentic AI, and the Quiet Collapse of Judgment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This essay is a theoretical and philosophical analysis drawing exclusively on published sources and publicly available documents. It does not involve human participants, personal data, empirical research, or experimental procedures. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted as part of the author's regular research activities at INSEEC Business School.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the rise of agentic AI—systems capable of autonomous perception, planning, and action—poses a structural threat to democratic life that conventional AI ethics frameworks fail to diagnose. Drawing on Hannah Arendt's analyses of totalitarianism, the vita activa, and the banality of evil, the paper identifies the deepest risk of agentic AI not as misalignment but as axiological displacement: the systematic transformation of what a society recognises as valuable through the progressive delegation of judgment to autonomous systems.
The paper makes three contributions. First, it establishes an Arendtian diagnostic framework for agentic AI, showing that these systems reproduce the cognitive conditions Arendt identified as precursors to democratic collapse—not through terror, but by rendering independent thought structurally optional. Second, it introduces the concept of axiological displacement to describe how AI systems do not merely optimise within existing value frameworks but progressively reconstruct what counts as a value, extending Arendt's analysis of superfluousness into the domain of algorithmic governance. Third, it demonstrates that social media platforms are neurologically preparing the next generation for this delegation, drawing on longitudinal neurodevelopmental research to argue that algorithmic atrophy of prefrontal judgment capacities and the deployment of agentic AI constitute two phases of a single process.
The paper concludes that AI governance must move beyond calibration and alignment toward the preservation of institutional spaces for genuine human deliberation, proposing axiological impact assessments as a necessary complement to the existing regulatory framework.

title: High-Quality Economic Development and the Mechanism of Innovation Transmission: A Study of Chinese Manufacturing Firms
affiliations: and Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) - Graduate School of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences

detail.title: High-Quality Economic Development and the Mechanism of Innovation Transmission: A Study of Chinese Manufacturing Firms
detail.abstract: Drawing on long-term micro-level data of Chinese manufacturing firms, this paper systematically examines the mechanisms of innovation transmission across industries and firms from the perspective of organizational structure. Innovation is embedded into a dynamic system comprising firm size distribution, ownership networks, and asset accumulation, and an analytical framework of “size structure–ownership network–asset accumulation” is constructed. The findings are as follows. First, the thick-tailed distribution of firm size leads to a persistent concentration of innovation resources in leading firms. Scale advantages are endogenously transformed into stable technological barriers through mechanisms such as R&D cost advantages and technological trajectories, resulting in a hierarchical transmission pattern of innovation driven by core firms. Second, ownership networks play a pivotal hub role in innovation transmission. Large enterprise groups amplify individual innovations into system-wide spillovers through coordinated R&D decisions and unified technological standards. Third, initial asset accumulation is transformed into long-term innovation advantages through intertemporal mechanisms, including sustained R&D investment, enhancement of organizational capabilities, and absorption of external technologies, demonstrating a pronounced cumulative effect. Overall, innovation transmission in Chinese manufacturing exhibits significant structural and network characteristics, with a dynamic pattern characterized by persistent concentration and hierarchical diffusion of innovation advantages across firms.

title: Information Geometry of Learned Financial Representations: Curvature, Tail Risk, and Stability

detail.title: Information Geometry of Learned Financial Representations: Curvature, Tail Risk, and Stability
detail.abstract:
We develop an information-geometric framework for analyzing learned financial representations and their impact on tail-risk sensitivity. Modeling predictive systems as mappings from inputs to probability laws, we study the Fisher geometry induced by learned distributions and its interaction with coherent risk measures. 
We characterize geodesics and curvature of the statistical manifold and show that sectional curvature governs second-order sensitivity of tail-risk functionals. In particular, negative curvature leads to nonlinear amplification of Expected Shortfall and spectral risk measures along representation drift trajectories. 
The analysis yields geometric diagnostics including Fisher drift and curvature-adjusted stability scores, providing practical tools for monitoring representation stability. We interpret the results in relation to optimal transport robustness and modern model risk frameworks, positioning information geometry as a natural complement to distributional stability and risk-sensitive control perspectives.

title: Valuing Inflation-linked Retirement Income in India
affiliations: Samasthiti Advisors and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Valuing Inflation-linked Retirement Income in India
detail.abstract:
The simple goal for retirees is to maintain pre-retirement consumption and hence they require assured real retirement income. This goal is also clearly articulated in Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority’s (PFRDA) recent Consultation Paper (see PFRDA 2025). But there is no observable real yield curve in India because of an absence of inflation-indexed government instruments from which the cost of a real pension can be directly inferred. This absence makes it difficult to assess how inflation-linked retirement income should be priced by Pension Fund Managers (PFMs) and consequently, how much capital a retiree must commit, over their lifecycle, to secure a guaranteed real pension.

This paper develops and applies two complementary approaches to estimate the cost of inflation-linked retirement income in India to help stakeholders arrive at unbiased estimates of the price of real retirement income. The first approach constructs a shadow real yield curve by overlaying stochastic inflation dynamics on the observed nominal government bond yield curve. The second approach introduces a stochastic asset–liability framework—CALMS (unConventional Asset–Liability Pricing Model using Stochastic techniques)—in which a dynamically managed equity–debt portfolio is explicitly designed to deliver inflation-adjusted retirement income. Under this approach, the price of real retirement income is imputed from the minimum portfolio size required to sustain real payouts subject to a specified failure-probability constraint.

Together, these approaches provide consistent and economically intuitive estimates of the cost of real retirement income in India. The results offer a practical benchmark for retirees, policymakers, and pension designers seeking to evaluate inflation-linked pensions in an environment where market-implied real yields are unavailable.

title: Operationalizing Fit in Recruitment: A Multi-KPI, Evidence-Based Matching Architecture
affiliations: Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., LUM University Giuseppe Degennaro, Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l. and Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l.

detail.title: Operationalizing Fit in Recruitment: A Multi-KPI, Evidence-Based Matching Architecture
detail.abstract: The current study proposes a multi-KPI approach for the alignment of job offers with candidate profiles that combines semantic signals, skill coverage indicators, and behavioral/contextual dimensions into a single decision support architecture. The approach is based on a semantic-first paradigm that represents job offers and candidate profiles as text embeddings that can be compared using the cosine similarity measure to produce a scalable baseline ranking that remains robust across different languages and styles. The baseline approach can then be extended using additional KPIs that capture different dimensions of the candidate-job alignment: the Hard Skill Coverage Ratio (HSCR) and the Skill Gap Index (SGI) measure the satisfaction of hard skill requirements and the remaining skill gaps; the Hard Skill Proficiency Similarity (HSPS) measures semantic similarity in the hard skill domain; the Soft Skill Semantic Alignment (SSSA) and the Soft Skill Evidence Density (SSED) measure the semantic similarity of the candidate behavior and the quality of the corroborating evidence; the Cultural & Team Fit Score (CTFS) addresses the organizational fit; and other indicators cover the operational feasibility of the candidate-job match. The approach is implemented using Python and tested using a realistic testbed of 300 EURES job postings and 300 heterogeneous candidate profiles across different formats and languages. The results show that the semantic approach yields a stable baseline that can be used to produce coherent and well-ordered shortlists of candidate-job pairs while the additional KPIs improve the interpretability of the approach and the feasibility of constraint satisfaction. The analysis of the candidate-job scores and the separations of the rankings also reveals that there are clusters of technically equivalent candidates and that there are clear cases of dominance. Overall, the approach can support an incremental move toward multicriteria decision making while balancing scalability, transparency, and governance-by-design requirements.

title: Long-Term Breakeven Inflation Rates and Federal Reserve Treasury Market Actions: 2018- 2024
affiliations: Boise State University and Texas Tech University

detail.title: Long-Term Breakeven Inflation Rates and Federal Reserve Treasury Market Actions: 2018- 2024

publicationDetails.detailsText: No, this is a working paper being submitted to journals.

detail.abstract: We examine how Federal Reserve actions in Treasury markets shaped market-based measures of long-term inflation expectations from 2018 through 2024. Using daily breakeven inflation (BEI) rates at 5-and 10-year horizons, we compare QE4 with the periods immediately before and after. During QE4, BEI exhibited heightened volatility and a breakdown in the usual correlation between nominal and real yields. Fed purchases of nominal Treasuries significantly reduced BEI, while TIPS purchases raised it. These effects are robust across data frequencies, indicating that BEI during QE4 reflected Federal Reserve balance sheet composition rather than solely market-driven expectations.

title: Modelling Heterogeneity in Panel Data for the Governance Climate and Human Development in Relation to Economic Growth and Sociocultural Factors: An Empirical Investigation across MEDA Transitional Economies
affiliations: University of Perugia

detail.title: Modelling Heterogeneity in Panel Data for the Governance Climate and Human Development in Relation to Economic Growth and Sociocultural Factors: An Empirical Investigation across MEDA Transitional Economies
detail.abstract: This paper examined the governance climate-growth nexus and governance climate-human development nexus in relation to sociocultural factors, using panel data over the period 1996-2019 across MEDA transitional economies. The study employed random-effect models and a probit model with sample selection. Additionally, the Dumitrescu-Hurlin (DH) test was computed to assess statistical precedence between the governance climate and human development. Our results suggest that past governance and development conditions, controlling for sociocultural factors, are significant determinants of the current state of governance climate and human development in MEDA transitional economies. Meanwhile, economic growth, as measured by per-capita GDP, does not appear to have a significant direct influence in our models. The timetrend has a negative effect on both governance climate and human development, highlighting the decline of their development-path over time. The most influential sociocultural factors found in the models were power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertain avoidance, and indulgence. However, a significant selection-bias term in the probit model highlights the heterogeneity characterizing the MEDA countries sample. Finally, the DH-test shows that there is no bidirectional causality between governance climate and human development, instead human development precedes governance climate in all MEDA transitional economies. In conclusion, our findings provide valuable insights into the macro-factors that shape governance climate and human development in MEDA transitional economies.

title: SET
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics and Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: SET
detail.abstract: We develop a novel theoretical framework-the Sign-Equivalent Transformation (SET)-to analyze the mathematical structure of non-linear equilibrium systems. SET formalizes the invariance of equilibrium solutions under a class of admissible transformations and thereby provides a unified methodology for studying a broad range of economic models. We illustrate its scope by applying it to settings such as production networks, trade, spatial models, non-linear peer effects, oligopoly competition, network games, and multiplex environments. We introduce two families of nonlinear network games-one capturing strategic complementarities and the other capturing strategic substitutes-within which standard models arise as special cases. Using SET, we establish existence and uniqueness and derive new equilibrium characterization results.

title: Bank Fragility, Lender of Last Resort, and Liquidity Regulation
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, European Central Bank, Financial Research Division and University of Bristol Business School

detail.title: Bank Fragility, Lender of Last Resort, and Liquidity Regulation
detail.abstract: We examine how a lender of last resort (LLR) and liquidity regulation jointly shape bank fragility when both liquidity and debt pricing are endogenous. In a global-games model of rollover risk, a bank's ex-ante fragility-the probability of a run-depends on how liquidity choices interact with the pricing of short-term debt. We show that LLR policy on its own can backfire: by reducing incentives to self-insure with liquid reserves, it raises debt burdens and amplifies fragility. Minimum liquidity requirements counteract this effect by strengthening balance-sheet resilience and making central-bank support more targeted. Together, the two instruments deliver greater stability and welfare than either in isolation. The analysis highlights a new micro-prudential role for liquidity regulation-enhancing the social value of the LLR.

title: A Competition Law Perspective on Why Non-Compete Clauses in Employment Contracts Should be Banned
affiliations: University of East Anglia (UEA) - Centre for Competition Policy

detail.title: A Competition Law Perspective on Why Non-Compete Clauses in Employment Contracts Should be Banned
detail.abstract: This article examines the status of non-compete clauses (NCCs) in employment contracts through the lens of competition law. Although traditionally governed in England and Wales by the common law restraint of trade doctrine, NCCs have attracted increasing scrutiny amid concerns about their labour market effects. While competition authorities have treated wage-fixing and no-poach agreements as restrictions of competition by object under Article 101 TFEU and the Competition Act 1998, NCCs generally fall outside competition where they are applied to employment contracts. The article argues, however, that NCCs share material similarities with labour market cartels and generate comparable distortions, including suppressed wages and reduced mobility. Applying the principle of ancillary restraints, it contends that employment NCCs are equivalent to practices that have as their object the significant restriction of competition. Given the availability of less restrictive means to protect legitimate employer interests, the article concludes that incremental reform is inadequate and advocates a comprehensive statutory ban in the UK.

title: Dynamics between India and Other Emerging Economies of the World during Major Crises
affiliations: Poornaprajna Institute of Management, Udupi

detail.title: Dynamics between India and Other Emerging Economies of the World during Major Crises
detail.abstract: The dynamic conditional correlations and covariances between the stock markets of India and the economies of 12 emerging nations (Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, Brazil, Russia, China, South Africa, Mexico, Argentina, Indonesia and Turkey) were studied. The study used a Multivariate Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity model (DCC MGARCH). The daily closing prices data of the stock exchanges for each country were collected for 14 years, from 2nd April 2007 to 1st April 2021. For analysis purposes, the 12 economies were divided into subgroups of 4 and compared with the Indian market. The results indicate that the linkages between India and the other emerging markets are strongest during crises. The portfolio diversification benefits exist in the short term only. Linkages are strongest within Asia, barring China. A portfolio of India and China can give stable returns as the associations between the two economies remain low even during periods of the financial crisis. The time-varying nature of the financial integration process further points to the markets' adaptation to new information, leaving doors open for active portfolio management.

title:
Does ESG Information Increase Crash Risk? 

Evidence on Monitoring from Credit Lines and Governance by Institutional Investors
affiliations: Sapporo University

detail.title:
Does ESG Information Increase Crash Risk? 

Evidence on Monitoring from Credit Lines and Governance by Institutional Investors
