declarations.funderStatement: The author is grateful to the Small and Medium Sized M&A Research and Education Center at Kobe University for providing data support. This research was also supported by the 2024 Research Grant Program of Sapporo University. Any remaining errors are the author’s own.

detail.abstract: Using 3,923 firm-year observations from 2016 to 2025 in Japan, we provide evidence that ESG scores are positively associated with crash risk for firms with greater access to credit lines and fewer institutional ownership. The effect of credit lines appears to operate through monitoring. However, this monitoring primarily targets ESG-related activities rather than liquidity, as it is not mitigated by higher operating cash flow and a larger unused credit line. Moreover, this effect cannot be fully mitigated by increased information quality, as it remains significant for both green bond-issued firms and firms with third-party certification. In contrast, institutional investors play a more prominent role for firms without green bond issuance or third-party certification, highlighting the importance of corporate governance when ESG information is subject to limited external assurance. Finally, we observe a substitution effect by governance, as credit lines play a stronger monitoring role in firms with fewer bank and trust investors.

title: Structural and Systemic Racism: An Analytic Framework for Measurement and Policy Intervention
affiliations: Emory University - Department of Economics, University of Michigan and Johns Hopkins School of Education

detail.title: Structural and Systemic Racism: An Analytic Framework for Measurement and Policy Intervention
detail.abstract:
Structural and systemic racism are widely invoked in health research, yet they are often left definitionally amorphous or used interchangeably, creating confusion about what to measure and where to intervene. Empirical studies commonly summarize
"structural racism'' with an index and then use it to predict a single downstream health outcome--which may itself help constitute structural racism--creating endogeneity problems with little actionable policy guidance.  Health-equity scholarship has increasingly called for systems approaches to map feedbacks and leverage points, but has not yet translated those insights into measurement-ready analytic criteria for prioritizing policy interventions against structural racism.

     We introduce Justice Under Dependent Outcomes (JUDO), a formal framework for resolving these conceptual, measurement, and policy challenges.  Building on existing definitions in the literature, JUDO formalizes structural and systemic racism as distinct but nested characterizations that sometimes coincide, with analytic expressions that guide measurement and intervention. In an illustrative example motivated by myocardial infarction inequities, we demonstrate how inter-institutional link strength shapes both index misestimation and the optimal points of policy intervention. In doing so, we show not only that addressing a smaller upstream inequity can reduce total inequity more than correcting a larger downstream one, but also explicit conditions under which this reversal occurs.  The framework shifts analysis from using structural racism indices to explain health outcomes towards the systematic identification of high leverage points against structural racism itself.

title: Belt and Road Initiative from the Perspective of the Philippines: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Future

detail.title: Belt and Road Initiative from the Perspective of the Philippines: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Future
detail.abstract: The dual-pronged Belt and Road Initiative has promises for relatively young modern infrastructures in the Philippines. The Sin0-Philippine ties are rooted in the pre-colonial voyages of the Chinese to the archipelago. To current bilateral agreements, advancing the Maritime Silk Road would create greater opportunities in green energy, the digital Silk  Road, and the current Philippine Government's thrust on Build Better More (BBM). Challenges like policy shifts and South China Sea tensions can be overcome through the institutionalization of policies, the localization of agreements, and the establishment of sustainable frameworks.

title: Institutional Shocks and Migration Adjustment: Evidence from the Syrian Crisis and Brexit’s Referendum and Implementation
affiliations: Tel Aviv University - Eitan Berglas School of Economics

detail.title: Institutional Shocks and Migration Adjustment: Evidence from the Syrian Crisis and Brexit’s Referendum and Implementation
detail.abstract:
This paper interprets Brexit as a two-stage institutional rupture that reshaped migration through expectations, exposure, and stress channels. Using a UK–Germany Difference-in-Differences framework, I show that the 2016 referendum generated a sharp decline in UK net migration relative to Germany, driven primarily by a contraction in immigration rather than simple outward flight. The 2021 termination of EU free movement reinforced this adjustment on the gross inflow margin, completing the structural reallocation of mobility flows. Migration responses were not uniform: countries more deeply integrated into EU mobility networks prior to 2016 experienced significantly stronger contractions, confirming that Brexit propagated along pre-existing exposure channels.Embedding macro-financial stress interactions reveals that institutional fragility amplified the referendum shock, particularly during the expectations phase. Stress intensified migration contractions in exposed settings in 2016, while post-2021 responses became more heterogeneous, especially on the emigration margin. Together, the results support a sequential interpretation: an anticipatory expectations shock in 2016 followed by regime completion in 2021.Beyond short-run behavioral adjustments, the findings are consistent with the fiscal self-selection framework. Increases in perceived institutional risk alter the relative returns to skill and investment, reshaping both the composition of migration and foreign direct investment. Because skilled labor and FDI are complementary, institutional credibility shocks can generate self-reinforcing declines in human capital inflows and investment. Brexit therefore emerges not merely as a trade or regulatory event, but as an institutional credibility shock in which migration operates both as an outcome and as a transmission mechanism linking regime change to long-run growth dynamics.

title: Dollarization Waves: New Evidence From a Comprehensive International Bond Database
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Cornell University - Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management, Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Dollarization Waves: New Evidence From a Comprehensive International Bond Database
detail.abstract:
We investigate how the U.S. dollar’s prominence in the denomination of international debt securities has evolved in recent decades, using a comprehensive global dataset with far more extensive coverage than datasets used in prior literature. We find no monotonic dollarization or de-dollarization trend; instead, the dollar’s share exhibits a wavelike pattern. We document three dollarization waves since the 1960s. The last wave, following the global financial crisis, lifted the dollar’s share nearly back to its level at the euro’s launch in 2000. We show that closer alignment of a country’s domestic currency to a reserve currency (e.g., the U.S. dollar) correlates with higher shares of issuance in that currency. Our findings are robust to composition and currency valuation effects as well as alternative data definitions.

title: Market Feedback about Emerging Technologies

detail.title: Market Feedback about Emerging Technologies
detail.abstract:
How do firms make decisions on investments in emerging technologies? We find that firms adjust AI/green investments in response to market reactions to announcements of such emerging-technology investment plans. Through a battery of tests, we show that this pattern is more likely due to active managerial learning from the market than alternative explanations such as a passive reflection of underlying fundamentals that drive both market reactions and corporate actions. Firms are more likely to act on feedback about emerging technologies than about other investments, particularly when market participants have more expertise in these areas and when firms face greater uncertainty.

title: Market Integration, Ambiguity, and Expected Returns: Evidence from the Stock Connect in China
affiliations: City University of Macau and The Australian National University

detail.title: Market Integration, Ambiguity, and Expected Returns: Evidence from the Stock Connect in China
detail.abstract: We study whether equity-market integration reduces ambiguity and whether integration changes how ambiguity is priced. Using China's Shanghai-Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect program, we exploit staggered, rule-based expansions of Stock Connect as a quasi-experiment. We measure stock-level ambiguity using high-frequency intraday returns based on the Brenner-Izhakian ambiguity measure. Heterogeneity-robust staggered differencein-differences and Sun-Abraham interaction-weighted event studies show that eligibility significantly lowers ambiguity; the decline is larger for stocks that were ex ante more illiquid, although liquidity proxies in the first stage move in mixed directions. In pricing tests, ambiguity predicts future returns, and Stock Connect inclusion lowers the ambiguity premium for eligible stocks. We also find that integration increases the sensitivity of stocklevel ambiguity to global policy uncertainty, consistent with a shift in the composition of uncertainty that investors price. Overall, the evidence suggests that Stock Connect compresses local probability instability while redirecting attention toward global sources of model uncertainty that matter for expected returns.

title: The Changing Landscape of International Development: An Introduction
affiliations: Princeton University, Yale University - Department of Economics and Yale University - Economic Growth Center

detail.title: The Changing Landscape of International Development: An Introduction
detail.abstract:
Since the late 1980s, extreme poverty has declined sharply, life expectancy and schooling have increased, and electoral democracy has expanded. However poverty reduction has slowed in recent years, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic, amid intensifying conflict, fragility, climate risks, democratic backsliding, and the erosion of global trends—including trade integration and geopolitical stability—that once supported growth. These dynamics raise three interrelated questions: what barriers impede further progress; where will future growth in lower-income countries come from; and how can growth be broadly shared. Taking stock of 15 chapters forthcoming in Volume 6 of the Handbook of Development Economics, we discuss how external conditions, state capacity and policy choices shape development; analyze the shifting growth drivers, including trade, technology and the rise of services; discuss persistent inequality and distributional tensions; and conjecture that investing in institutions and people pays off.

title: The Elasticity of Corporate Taxable Income Across Countries
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, ZEW Mannheim, ESSEC Business School - Finance Department, , University of Notre Dame - Department of Economics, Utah State University, World Bank, Government Office of the Slovak Republic, Universidad Nacional de La Plata (UNLP), The World Bank, Duke University, Charles University, Hellenic Open University, Prague University of Economics and Business, , CUNEF Universidad, , University of Lisbon - ISEG School of Economics and Management, Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer, University of Mannheim, Northeastern University, Charles University, University of Duisburg-Essen, Leibniz University Hannover, World Bank and

detail.title: The Elasticity of Corporate Taxable Income Across Countries
detail.abstract:
Do firms respond similarly to corporate tax incentives across countries? We provide globally comparable estimates of the corporate elasticity of taxable income using administrative tax return data from sixteen countries and a unified empirical framework. Exploiting bunching at a common kink, zero taxable income, we estimate elasticities ranging from 0.08 to 1.9, with an average of 0.79. To explain this heterogeneity, we link elasticities to tax policy, firm characteristics, and country fundamentals. These differences imply that identical corporate tax reforms can generate sharply different revenue effects across countries, leading to substantial heterogeneity in the efficiency costs of corporate taxation.

title: "Feel" as a Determinant of College Choice: Evidence from Campus Tour Weather
affiliations: Amherst College, Amherst College and Amherst College

detail.title: "Feel" as a Determinant of College Choice: Evidence from Campus Tour Weather
detail.abstract:
The feeling or impression that students get about enrolling in a particular college may be an important determinant of their college application decision. Combining institutional records on college campus tour participants over the last decade with hourly weather information, we leverage tour weather as a plausibly exogenous shock to students' "feel" for attending the toured college. We find that poor tour weather reduces participants’ likelihood of applying. Tour participants, for example, are 10 percent less likely to apply when their tour is hot and 8 percent less likely when precipitation occurs during their tour. Using administrative data documenting where all tour participants enroll in college, we find that tour weather has little to no impact on the quality or type of college that participants ultimately attend. Nevertheless, our results suggest that students' "feel" for attending a college can play an important role in the college application decision.

title: National Identity as Economic Infrastructure; Why Alignment between State Power and a People's Lived Identity Determines Prosperity or Collapse
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: National Identity as Economic Infrastructure; Why Alignment between State Power and a People's Lived Identity Determines Prosperity or Collapse
detail.abstract: Economic stability and long-term prosperity depend not only on capital, institutions, or policy choices, but on the degree of alignment between political authority and the lived national identity of the population it governs. This paper advances a comparative analytical framework in which national identity functions as an economic coordination mechanism: when political power is perceived as representing a shared identity, legitimacy is sustained, coordination costs remain low, and long-horizon economic activity becomes viable; when that alignment erodes or is replaced by imposed ideology, coordination costs rise, legitimacy weakens, and economic outcomes deteriorate even in materially well-endowed states.

title: The Heterogeneous Earnings Impact of Job Loss Across Workers, Establishments, and Markets
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Revelio Labs, Uppsala University, Uppsala University and Uppsala University

detail.title: The Heterogeneous Earnings Impact of Job Loss Across Workers, Establishments, and Markets
detail.abstract:
Using rich Swedish administrative data, we apply causal machine learning methods to study how earnings losses after job displacement vary with observable characteristics that may be relevant for targeting policy interventions for workers. Heterogeneity in effects is as large within as across worker groups defined by age and schooling, and as large within as across establishments. A substantial portion of cross-establishment heterogeneity can be explained by industry and local labor market characteristics, suggesting a role for place- and industry-based targeting. The largest losses are concentrated among already vulnerable workers, indicating that well-designed targeting policies can improve both efficiency and equity.

title: The Role Of Basic Education In Humen-Centred Development
affiliations: Mongolian national defense university and Mongolian national defense university

detail.title: The Role Of Basic Education In Humen-Centred Development
detail.abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence, when development and innovation are being discussed in all sectors, the question arises as to whether sustainable development will be focused on people or on artificial intelligence. In Mongolia, the government has declared 2026 the "Year of Education" and the Defence sector the "Year of Human-Centred Development and Innovation", which has led to discussions about the future development of education and innovation in the educational sphere. Therefore, we will develop a new, improved experiment based on the results and experience of previous studies on the topic "The role of basic education in human-centred development", based on the example of probability theory, mathematical statistics courses, as well as the results and experience of previous studies on human-centred approaches to learning, team teaching methods, future educational trends, the use of artificial intelligence and ethical responsibility. As part of this study, we prepared the results of three pilot lessons from the course "Probability theory, Mathematical Statistics" conducted jointly by six teachers from the Mongolian National Defence University (MNDU), with the participation and feedback of 90 students.

title: Exploring ChatGPT Adoption Among Teacher Educators in Higher Education: An Extended UTAUT2 Approach

detail.title: Exploring ChatGPT Adoption Among Teacher Educators in Higher Education: An Extended UTAUT2 Approach
detail.abstract: Technology adoption among individuals is driven by behavioural intention (BI), which is influenced by multiple factors. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology2 (UTAUT2) is a framework for understanding the determinants of BI towards acceptance and usage of technology. With ChatGPT being one of the most widely adopted OpenAI tools among Indians, this study employed the UTAUT2 model to examine its adoption among teacher educators (TEs) of higher education institutions. The findings revealed that Effort Expectancy was the most significant factor in facilitating TEs' BI to adopt ChatGPT, followed by Performance Expectancy. Credibility, price value, and hedonic motivation also played a substantial role in influencing TEs' adoption behaviour. Furthermore, the study found that Social Influence had a notable impact on TEs' BI in adopting ChatGPT, whereas Facilitating Conditions contributed minimally to their adoption decisions. This study is significant as it utilised the said model to explore the BI of Indian higher education educators towards ChatGPT. This is an understudied demographic segment in the Indian context, making the findings insightful.

title: Political Party Influence on Renewable Portfolio Standards: A Panel Data Analysis of U.S. States (2001-2024)
affiliations: University of Texas

detail.title: Political Party Influence on Renewable Portfolio Standards: A Panel Data Analysis of U.S. States (2001-2024)
detail.abstract: The effect of political Governor or party on Renewable Portfolio Standard adoption is examined across 50 U.S. states from 2001 to 2024. Using fixed-effects panel regression with clustered standard errors, it is found that persistent Democratic control has a small positive and statistically insignificant effect on RPS adoption (β = 0.047, SE = 0.045). While lagged party control shows a statistically significant impact. Specifically, two(β =0.004) and three(β =0.006) year Democratic control lag is associated with higher RPS levels compared to Republican control, which affirms policy lag hypothesis. Electricity prices show a positive result with RPS (pre-2009: β = 0.035, p < 0.05; post-2009: β = 0.018, p < 0.05). In contrast, the effect of GDP per capita remains mixed and statistically insignificant. The Hausman test confirms the superiority of the fixed-effects model over random effects (χ² = 49.53, p < 0.001). Structural break tests using the Bai-Perron method identify two major shifts in 2007 and 2015, while Chow tests indicate that the effect of party control on RPS did not significantly differ before and after 2009 (χ² = 0.93, p = 0.335). These results affirm the policy feedback framework, highlighting that institutional inertia and lagged political influence shape renewable policy outcomes over time. Finally, Bai-Perron multiple structural break test to investigate the temporal variability in the factors influencing Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) adoption across U.S. states from 2001 to 2024. The findings of this study contradict the null hypothesis of parameter stability, thereby identifying two statistically significant structural breaks in 2007 and 2015.

title: UIRAM: An Intention-Uncertainty-Based Risk Assessment Framework for Interactive Traffic Scenarios
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Intelligent Systems Engineering

detail.title: UIRAM: An Intention-Uncertainty-Based Risk Assessment Framework for Interactive Traffic Scenarios
detail.abstract: The growing heterogeneity of driving behaviors makes accurate identification and quantitative assessment of imminent collisions a cornerstone of safety assurance. Yet existing risk detection and scoring methods generalize poorly across complex scenarios and often disregard uncertainty in surrounding agents’ intentions. To bridge this gap, we propose UIRAM, an uncertain-intention-based risk assessment method for interactive traffic participants. UIRAM first rapidly selects collision-relevant candidates using a simplified 2D Gaussian conflict field, then infers each participant’s intention distribution together with a calibrated uncertainty estimate via an intention prediction network that fuses environmental context and interaction dynamics. Leveraging these outputs, we compute the collision probability between the ego vehicle and each candidate and aggregate probability with consequence severity to derive an overall risk score, using the maximum per-agent risk as the scenario-level indicator. Experiments on the FLUID dataset show that UIRAM achieves at least a 0.22% AUC improvement over representative baselines (PODAR, DRAC, and THW) while completing per-vehicle uncertainty prediction and risk computation within 0.14 s. Driver-in-the-loop simulations further confirm strong agreement between UIRAM’s risk scores and drivers’ subjective risk perception.

title: Restricting Rights, Preserving Inequalities: When Microaggressions Function as Tools to MaintainAableist and Sexist Hegemonies
affiliations: and Kobe University

detail.title: Restricting Rights, Preserving Inequalities: When Microaggressions Function as Tools to MaintainAableist and Sexist Hegemonies

declarations.funderStatement: We are deeply grateful to the funding from a research grant awarded by the University of the Philippines Center for Women’s and Gender Studies (UP CWGS).

detail.abstract: How do microaggressions directed at Filipino women with mobility disabilities function as mechanisms of oppression that simultaneously restrict their exercise of fundamental human rights and maintain systems of ableist and sexist hegemonies? We aim to address this question by focusing on the qualitative data obtained from a focus group discussion with 10 women with mobility disabilities from Tahanang Walang Hagdanan, Inc., to elucidate the link between microaggressions and inequalities. Using feminist disability studies and faces of oppression as theoretical lens, we identified two overarching themes: (1) Microaggressions as tools to limit rights enjoyment: demonstrates how microaggressions restrict women with mobility disabilities' enjoyment of human rights; and (2) Microaggressions as tools to maintain existing inequalities: shows how microaggressions preserve existing hegemonic power structures that privilege able-bodied individuals and patriarchal norms. Building on these findings, we argue that microaggressions are not subtle nor isolated incidents all the time. They vary across certain spaces and times, and their nuances make them implicit tools to maintain ableist and sexist hegemonies. There is a need to problematise microaggressions as actual problems embedded in social structures that have been normalised. Moreover, revealing their complexities and ambiguities is necessary rather than accepting them as "unintended consequences" of social inclusion. We posit the urgency to critically discuss how microaggressions that occur in public and private spaces must be addressed in context-specific manners. title: Lagged Competitive Displacement: Higher-Order Evidence for Zero-Sum Transatlantic Productivity Dynamics

detail.title: Lagged Competitive Displacement: Higher-Order Evidence for Zero-Sum Transatlantic Productivity Dynamics
detail.abstract: A previous paper documented that European productivity acceleration responds at only one-third the rate of United States acceleration in technologyintensive sectors, interpreting this as "differential growth rather than zero-sum reallocation." This follow-up paper challenges that interpretation. Using an expanded panel of 480 observations across six 2-digit codes from the Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community (NACE) and five European economies, higher-order derivative analysis reveals that the lagged thirdorder relationship is negative: when United States productivity acceleration increases in period t, European productivity acceleration decreases in period t + 1 (β =-0.34, p < 0.001). The zero-sum hypothesis is confirmed. United States productivity gains do come at Europe's expense, but the competitive displacement operates through lagged higherorder dynamics rather than contemporaneous correlations. Short-run co-movement masks the underlying inverse relationship that emerges with a oneperiod lag at the third derivative.

title: Law, Ethics, and Judicial Control of Court Proceedings: A Doctrinal Reappraisal of Equality, Seniority, and Precedence at the Nigerian Bar

detail.abstract: This study is prompted by the controversy that arose from proceedings sometime ago at the High Court of Enugu State sitting at Oji River, publicly narrated by a counsel and subsequently debated within the Bar, which transformed routine courtroom practices involving seating arrangements and calling cases out of turn into a wider legal and ethical dispute, thereby exposing persistent uncertainties and misconceptions within the profession, regarding the legal foundations of professional hierarchy, the meaning and scope of equality at the Bar, and the extent of judicial authority to manage court proceedings. Building on the factual narrative, statutory provisions, ethical rules, case law, the inherent jurisdiction of court, and professional debates generated by the incident, this study conducts a reassessment of the concepts of equality, seniority, precedence, and courtroom decorum in the Nigerian legal profession. The study shows that precedence is not an issue of courtesy or tradition but a legally mandated and ethically reinforced framework regulating professional relations at the Bar. Further, the study explains the practical operations of the rule of precedence, the non-absolute nature of the court's cause list, and the coordinating role of judicial discretion. The study advances a coherent framework for reconciling equality with hierarchy, and situates courtroom decorum within the discipline necessary for orderly adjudication.

title: Effect Of Social Media Marketing On Sme's Performance In Jalingo Lga, Taraba State
affiliations: Bayero University

detail.title: Effect Of Social Media Marketing On Sme's Performance In Jalingo Lga, Taraba State
detail.abstract: The study examined the effect of social media marketing on the performance of SMEs in Jalingo LGA, Taraba State. The data were analysed using a frequency table and percentages for descriptive statistics. Multiple regressions were used to analyse the objectives of the study. The findings indicated a significant positive effect of social media marketing on Facebook, WhatsApp, and Twitter on SMEs' performance in Jalingo LGA, Taraba State. Based on the findings, it was concluded that social media marketing has a significant effect on small business performance. The recommendations made, among others, were that since the findings revealed that social media advertising has momentous influence on small business performance in Jalingo LGA, Taraba State, it is recommended that the government should incorporate social media marketing in its various skills acquisition and entrepreneurship trainings because it was found to have a positive impact and provide an avenue for effective customer dealings. It will help small businesses establish a strategy to reach their customers easily through the use of WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter, and other social media marketing platforms, thereby increasing patronage of their products and services.

title: To Be or Not to Be a QDC? That is A Question: Qualifying Defence Contract Status under the Single Source Contract Regulations
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: To Be or Not to Be a QDC? That is A Question: Qualifying Defence Contract Status under the Single Source Contract Regulations
detail.abstract: In 2014, the Ministry of Defence introduced the Defence Reform Act and Single Source Contract Regulations to regulate the pricing and oversight of single source defence contracts. This is supported by the establishment of the Single Source Regulations Office. The regime is complex and has undergone ad hoc reform over the years. A decade on, with the regime bedding down, now is an opportune moment to take stock of its development. As a starting point, this article examines the issue of coverage from an academic perspective. It is argued that the rules and associated policies on coverage are too complex, too uncertain, and place too much unchecked discretion in the hands of the contracting parties. Further, recent reforms are inadequate and do not reflect the purported priorities to increase speed and simplification in accordance with broader defence industrial strategy. It follows that it is argued that there is, in principle, a case for further reform. Additional empirical research would help identify what is feasible in this regard.

detail.title: The EUREP Expansion and the Reconfiguration of International Dollar Backstops: Evidence of Regime Anticipation in Central Bank Facility Design

detail.abstract: On February 14, 2026, the European Central Bank announced that its Eurosystem Repo Facility for central banks (EUREP) would become a permanent, standing facility with global access from Q3 2026. This paper argues that the EUREP expansion is not a routine institutional upgrade but the first structural evidence that European monetary authorities are anticipating a regime change in the provision of international dollar liquidity. The announcement occurred fifteen days after the nomination of Kevin Warsh as Federal Reserve Chair-a nominee whose fifteen-year record of advocacy for a reduced Fed footprint raises fundamental questions about the future reliability of the dollar backstop architecture (swap lines, FIMA, balance sheet interventions) that the offshore dollar system has come to require. This paper documents the chronological sequence, analyses the structural parallels between EUREP and the Fed's FIMA facility, identifies the collateral depth asymmetry that limits the euro's capacity to serve as an alternative safe asset, and proposes a framework for interpreting EUREP as an instance 1 of "regime anticipation"-the phenomenon whereby institutional actors build alternative infrastructure not in response to a crisis that has occurred, but in preparation for a crisis response that might not come.

detail.abstract: This working paper examines the profound transformation of managerial function induced by the democratisation of artificial intelligence tools. Starting from Chandler's model of managerial capitalism, we analyse how AI triggers a major axiological displacement: it does not merely optimise existing managerial processes but fundamentally transforms what constitutes value in organisational coordination. Crucially, this displacement affects all levels of the managerial hierarchy, from middle managers to senior executives. We argue that AI reveals a fundamental distinction between owner-managers, whose legitimacy rests on capitalistic risk-bearing, and professional managers at all levels, whose legitimacy derived from expertise now commoditised by AI. This analysis suggests that AI may be reviving classical notions of ownership as the primary source of managerial authority, potentially reversing a century of managerial capitalism.

title: Network Motifs and the Rise of Entrepreneurial Ecosystems

detail.title: Network Motifs and the Rise of Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial ecosystem research has focused on macro-level configurations, yet the micro-level network structures underpinning ecosystem emergence remain underexplored. I introduce network motif analysis (the study of small recurring subgraphs) to entrepreneurial finance research, examining how emerging patterns in venture capital co-investment networks predict ecosystem rise. Analyzing 29 U.S. state ecosystems from 2015 to 2024, I identify distinct motif signatures for different trajectories. Booming ecosystems display squares and pentagons, i.e. extended trust chains reflecting "friends of friends of friends" logic. Established ecosystems exhibit triangles and hexagons, which are dense, orchestrated structures. Critically, heterogeneous motifs incorporating investors who differ by type, previous success rate, or vintage predict sustained growth more reliably than homogeneous patterns. These findings bridge micro-level network interdependencies with macro-level regional performance, offering policymakers actionable diagnostic tools for catalyzing entrepreneurial growth.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of social media platforms has fundamentally transformed communication dynamics globally. This study investigates the impact of communication skills on social media usage, emphasizing the moderating role of cultural restraint within the context of Jordan. Employing a quantitative research design, data were collected from 415 young adult social media users through an online survey and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 4 software. The findings suggest that individuals with strong communication skills are more effective at using social media, supporting the ideas of Self-Efficacy Theory and Social Capital Theory, which propose that better communication abilities lead to more proficient social media usage. However, this positive relationship is moderated by cultural restraint, with higher levels of cultural restraint weakening the impact of communication skills on social media engagement. These results highlight the necessity of culturally sensitive approaches when promoting social media engagement, as cultural norms and values significantly influence digital behaviors. This study contributes to the existing literature by providing empirical evidence from a non-Western context and underscores the complex interplay between individual abilities and cultural factors in shaping social media usage. Future research should explore additional moderating variables and consider longitudinal and cross-cultural studies to further elucidate these dynamics.

Adopting a structured model approach and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SMART PLS, this research uses 500 influencer posts from five Arab countries. The research adds a multidimensional framework for propelling AI into digital public communication in culturally sensitive and linguistically diverse environments and provides a blueprint for improving AI integration.

keywords: market learning JEL Codes: G14 (Information and Market Efficiency)

detail.abstract:
Ocean Tomo documents that intangible assets grew from 17% of S&P 500 market value in 1975 to 68% by 1995, crossing the 50% threshold in the early 1990s. This proportion has continued growing to 90% by 2020. The conventional explanation - that intangible assets "became more important" - is circular and fails to explain the reason, timing, mechanism, or persistence of this shift.

Building on Lo's (2004, 2017) Adaptive Markets Hypothesis, we propose that markets fundamentally changed their valuation methodology. Historically, company values were calculated using discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis alone. Since the mid-1990s, markets have adopted a hybrid valuation framework combining DCF for linear operations with real options valuation for embedded strategic optionality created by intangible assets. The value created by real options requires the existence of the real options, the ability to identify the real options by management, and, critically, the ability to exercise the real options properly.

What researchers call "intangible assets" (brands, R&D, customer relationships, platforms) create embedded real options - growth options, flexibility options, learning options, and platform options. These capabilities existed before 1995, but markets lacked the valuation framework to price the optionality they generated. The crossing of the 50% threshold in the early 1990s created salience that triggered valuation framework discovery. High-visibility exemplars (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) made option value legible, and the hybrid DCF + Options valuation framework diffused across sectors through the mid-to-late 1990s.

This valuation framework extends Lo's Adaptive Markets Hypothesis by specifying the learning mechanism: markets discover novel valuation frameworks when patterns cross salience thresholds. Rather than instantly pricing all available information as EMH assumes, markets require pattern salience before valuation framework discovery occurs. This reinterpretation also provides new perspective on "irrational exuberance", market bubbles, and “ridiculous” PE multiples, suggesting that what appeared as ridiculous valuations may have partly reflected rational options pricing during valuation framework learning, with behavioral overshoot as a smaller component. It also provides a mechanism to explain why companies with a history of losses can support multi-billion valuations.

Excerpt

Northern Paper

In May 2022, Blake Prescott, the controller for the Blue Ridge Mill, was considering the addition of a new on-site longwood woodyard. The addition would have two primary benefits: It would eliminate the need to purchase shortwood from an outside supplier, and it would create the opportunity to sell shortwood on the open market as a new market for Northern Paper. The new woodyard would allow the Blue Ridge Mill not only to reduce its operating costs but also to increase its revenues. The proposed woodyard would utilize new technology that allowed tree-length logs, called longwood, to be processed directly, whereas the current process required shortwood, which had to be purchased from the Shenandoah Mill. This nearby mill, owned by a competitor, had excess capacity that allowed it to produce more shortwood than it needed for its own pulp production. The excess was sold to several different mills, including the Blue Ridge Mill. Thus adding the new longwood equipment would mean that Prescott would no longer need to use the Shenandoah Mill as a shortwood supplier and that the Blue Ridge Mill would instead compete with the Shenandoah Mill by selling on the shortwood market. The question for Prescott was whether these expected benefits were enough to justify the $18 million capital outlay plus the incremental investment in working capital over the six-year life of the investment.

Construction would start within a few months, and the investment outlay would be spent over two calendar years: $16 million in 2022 and the remaining $2 million in 2023. When the new woodyard began operating in 2023, it would significantly reduce the operating costs of the mill. These operating savings would come mostly from the difference in the cost of producing shortwood on-site versus buying it on the open market; savings were estimated to be $2.0 million for 2023 and $3.5 million per year thereafter.

Prescott also planned on taking advantage of the excess production capacity afforded by the new facility by selling shortwood on the open market as soon as possible. For 2023, he expected to show revenues of approximately $2 million, as the facility came on line and began to break into the new market. He expected shortwood sales to reach $8 million in 2024 and continue at the $8 million level through 2028. Prescott estimated that the cost of goods sold (before including depreciation expenses) would be 75% of revenues, and selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses would be 10% of revenues.

title: What the History of Extinction Teaches Us: AI in Deep Historical Perspective
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: What the History of Extinction Teaches Us: AI in Deep Historical Perspective
detail.abstract:
Debates on artificial intelligence (AI) often focus on economic disruption, professional upheaval, algorithmic bias, privacy, safety, accountability, and governance. While these concerns are important in their own right, these concerns tend to emphasise narrowly defined technological risks over short timescales, especially when compared with the long history of life’s evolution, species survival, and extinction, including that of human ancestors. This policy brief offers a broader, long-term perspective grounded in deep history, drawing lessons from past episodes of human ancestor extinction. It highlights insights increasingly relevant today, particularly regarding AI’s influence on collective knowledge systems, its long-term effects on human expertise, epistemic concentration, the erosion of epistemic diversity and redundancy, and its role in reshaping collective cognition. It also considers how systemic fragility may develop gradually over time — a dimension largely absent from current AI debates. 

Research on cognition shows that thinking is embedded in everyday practices, tools, artefacts, and material interactions rather than confined to individual minds. Cognition emerges within systems of people, tools, practices, and environments. As AI becomes embedded in these systems, it increasingly shapes how knowledge is generated, interpreted, and applied. This raises a critical but underexplored governance question: how might AI affect the resilience, diversity, and interpretability of the knowledge systems on which societies depend? By linking deep historical insight to contemporary AI policy debates, this paper argues that the central challenge is not only to regulate AI as a powerful technology but also to safeguard the long-term robustness of collective knowledge systems. Ensuring interpretability, epistemic diversity, and institutional capacity is essential for maintaining meaningful human oversight in an increasingly AI-mediated world.

This case tells the true story of Doug Lebda, a Darden student inspired by an entrepreneurship course to start his own business, CreditSource USA. From Lebda's childhood learning sales from his father, to the genesis of his venture idea, to the hard work he put in putting the business plan together and trying to test its viability, the case explores Lebda's entrepreneurial path. Should he move forward with building CreditSource USA despite the disruption it might cause to his life...and the chance that he could fail at the endeavor?

Excerpt

CreditSource

It was almost the end of Doug Lebda's first year at the Darden School of Business (Darden). As he walked out of Jim Collins's class, he was full of excitement and determination. Collins had invited first-year students to sit in on the last day of a one-week entrepreneurship course he taught for second-year students. During this last session, Collins listed on the board every reason students came up with for not starting their dream venture. He then proceeded to cross them all out one by one, telling a story for each one about an entrepreneur who had done it in spite of that reason. Collins ended with the takeaway: “The risk is not that you're not going to succeed or fail, but that you're never gonna start.”

Lebda's heart raced as he thought, “Oh my God, I gotta do this.” Still, as he walked out of class, he knew he would have a tough row to hoe ahead of him. He would have to seek permission from faculty to take a leave of absence from Darden. More immediately, he needed to convince Tara, his wife of less than a year, that this was a good idea. Complicated thoughts and feelings rushed through him as he began tracing out a decision tree to help him decide whether to take the plunge.

Or not.

Doug Lebda, Accountant

After graduating from Bucknell University in 1992, Lebda joined PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in its Audit and Business Advisory Services group. He directed several debt and equity offerings, worked with development-stage clients, and gathered experience with derivative financial instruments. Lebda also gained experience in systems development working on a yearlong project for a Fortune 50 company that was developing interactive online manuals for over 100 domestic and international locations. While at PwC, Lebda developed marketing and sales expertise as he continually marketed PwC services to new and existing clients. This companion paper examines how the AI-driven workforce restructuring wave of 2025-2026 validates the framework's core predictions. Drawing on corporate actions by Block, McKinsey & Company, Accenture, Tata Consultancy Services, and others, this paper identifies three distinct phenomena being conflated under the umbrella of "AI layoffs," introduces the concept of "AI arbitrage" to describe how capital markets incentivize premature workforce reduction, and proposes a prescriptive sequencing model that ties headcount restructuring to verified capability rather than projected efficiency. The paper advances an 18-month correction hypothesis, examines the distinctive risks facing regulated industries, and extends the Intelligence Stack to individual career architecture. This analysis provides decision-makers, policymakers, and professionals with a structured lens for navigating the most significant workforce transformation since the Industrial Revolution.

detail.abstract:
Acceleration has become a defining condition of contemporary risk environments. Advances in artificial intelligence increasingly compress the time available for institutions to recognise signals, interpret conditions, decide, and act. Under these conditions, risk does not arise primarily from intent, error, or isolated shocks, but from structural mismatches between system velocity and institutional response capacity.

This paper introduces the concept of the velocity paradox: as capabilities accelerate, governance, coordination, and assurance mechanisms often lag, narrowing decision windows and eroding effective control. The analysis reframes acceleration not as speed alone, but as the rate of system change relative to institutional absorptive capacity.

To support this reframing, the paper presents the AETHERION Velocity Index as a diagnostic lens for identifying environments in which acceleration becomes a source of systemic risk. Rather than predicting outcomes, the framework highlights conditions under which margins for error compress, coupling effects intensify, and capacity shock emerges.

The paper applies this lens across geopolitics, compute infrastructure, climate constraint, cyber escalation, markets, and supply chains, showing how instability can arise without surprise, disruption, or hostile intent. The contribution is not prescriptive, but orientational: to support decision-makers in recognising when time itself becomes the binding constraint on governance, stability, and agency.

detail.abstract: Sustainable cloud adoption in developing regions requires policy frameworks that balance technological scalability, institutional capacity, and long-term public value. This paper proposes a policy-oriented framework for sustainable cloud adoption, grounded in a Ghana-based case study, to support resilient and inclusive digital transformation. Drawing on comparative policy analysis and existing cloud governance models, the study synthesizes institutional, regulatory, economic, and infrastructural considerations into an integrated adoption framework. The paper argues that cloud strategies in developing contexts must move beyond technology acquisition toward policy-driven implementation aligned with national development goals. Implications are discussed for policymakers, regulators, and organizational leaders seeking to design scalable and sustainable cloud adoption strategies in resource-constrained environments.

detail.title: Re-evaluating Diversification: The Evolving Role of Gaming in Market Turmoil
detail.abstract: Given gaming’s remarkable growth and its crucial role in the digital economy, this article examines volatility spillovers among this target sector, key industries (technology, semiconductor manufacturing, e-commerce & digital payments, communication services, consumer discretionary, consumer staples, utilities), and traditional financial assets (global equities, treasury bonds, real estate, gold). The analysis is carried out using the R2 decomposed connectedness approach and spans the period from January 1, 2015, to October 31, 2025. Results show strong interlinkages among markets, with e-commerce & digital payments and global equities being the main drivers of volatility transmission. We further evaluate the efficacy of portfolios integrated with gaming stocks for their hedging and diversification properties under varying market conditions. Our findings indicate that hedging is not an effective strategy during stable market conditions; however, other assets perform as significant diversifiers for gaming-focused portfolios. Nevertheless, during turbulent periods, gaming stocks transform into a potent hedge and safe haven for related industries, though not for conventional assets. This research provides critical insights for portfolio managers and institutional investors, advocating for an updated approach to risk management that accounts for the shifting correlation dynamics.

detail.abstract: This study investigates distributional heterogeneity in the relationship between financial literacy and demand-side financial development across Europe. Using microdata from Eurobarometer Flash Survey 525 (N = 24,356), we construct a latent household-level financial development variable via Polychoric Principal Component Analysis and Item Response Theory, then apply conditional quantile regression to estimate how the effect of financial literacy varies across the full distribution of household financial engagement. We document a structural "sticky floor": below the 20th percentile, financial literacy has no statistically discernible effect on financial development, reflecting a non-responsive zone driven by supply-side barriers rather than knowledge deficits. Above this zone, the marginal effect of financial literacy increases monotonically through the upper-middle quantiles before attenuating at the top-consistent with product saturation. A comparative analysis of Eastern and Western European subsamples reveals that this non-responsive zone extends significantly deeper in transition economies, where literacy effects remain statistically dormant until approximately the 40th percentile. These findings challenge the universalist framing of financial education policy and argue for sequenced interventions that prioritize structural access before broad-based literacy campaigns.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary models of political polarization frequently rely on individual psychology or game theory, assuming a neutral environment of communicative exchange. This paper proposes a structural alternative: that the “Backfire Effect” and the collapse of shared reality are not cognitive errors, but predictable geometric consequences of a High-Mass Information Topology that systematically filters out complex scientific discourse. By mapping the electorate onto a Social Manifold governed by principles isomorphic to General Relativity, we demonstrate that the “Stress-Energy” of the Algorithmic Attention Economy ($T_{μν}$) has warped the geometry of discourse beyond the critical limit of stability.

We define the “Orwell Limit,” a thermodynamic boundary condition derived from Landauer’s Principle, where the energy required to verify a fact exceeds the energy required to accept a falsehood. Utilizing Shannon Entropy to define “Informational Mass” and Statistical Mechanics to model the “Phase Transition” of the electorate, we prove that the velocity differential between High-Entropy Scientific Truth ($v \ll c$) and Low-Entropy Fabrication ($v \approx c$) creates a Causality Gap. The fabrication shapes the curvature of the manifold before the truth arrives to inhabit it, rendering objective verification thermodynamically inaccessible along the radicalized geodesic.

We conclude that the republic has entered a state of Metric Shear, fracturing the lattice into disjoint manifolds separated by an infinite cognitive distance. Remediation is no longer possible through persuasion; it requires a structural reconstruction of the topology itself, specifically, the imposition of Constitutional Latency and Informational Federalism to reduce the curvature of the social field and restore the geodesic required for scientific consensus.)

It notes that this emerging technology faces a number of regulatory challenges in terms of the legal disciplines of intellectual property, innovation law, and public health. detail.title: The Geoeconomics of the US and China

detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of slowbalization, but also growing bifurcation between the US and China, this chapter focuses on the economic realm of US–China strategic competition and what it means for the European Union. In the first section, it analyzes the areas where slowbalization—and in some cases deglobalization trends—is largest, from trade to supply chains and investment but with special focus on technology. Financial flows are so far less affected but with worrying signals, except for the COVID period for the latter, but the trend is that of bifurcation. This is also happening with people-to-people exchanges even after COVID. Finally, this chapter ponders the impact of this competition on the EU and offers ideas as to how the EU should react. The EU is obviously squeezed in a world of great power competition without room for multilateralism. It should leverage its economic size and its relatively developed technology to obtain the best terms possible for continuing to support the transatlantic Alliance while keeping markets open elsewhere. This includes China but with a view to reducing dependence on Chinese imports especially in the crucial sector of green tech, instrumental for Europe’s decarbonization. The EU’s continued quest for a stable and fruitful transatlantic Alliance is more realistic than that of strategic autonomy to achieve equidistance between the US and China. While it might be a Solomonic aspiration, it lacks realism in the current area of great power competition as an economic area without a central political power, an army, and with technology dependencies, mostly with the US.

title: China-Latin America Trade: Ever-growing Dependency

detail.title: China-Latin America Trade: Ever-growing Dependency
detail.abstract: Although the relationship between China and Latin America has many dimensions, trade is an area that has garnered considerable attention. Since the early 2000s, China’s double-digit growth rates and thirst for natural resources was behind the increase in trade between Latin America and China. Since 2017 onwards, China’s structural deceleration and, more recently, the collapse in China’s real estate has put a break on the country’s demand for commodities hurting Latin American exports to China. To further evaluate how much Latin American countries depend on commodities and on China for their trade, we develop a commodity dependency index, which enables us to take stock of Latin America’s shifting trade ties with China. We note that a few Latin countries have moved from commodity dependency to more complex integration into global value chains.

detail.abstract: We study the properties of macroeconomic survey forecast response averages as the number of survey respondents grows. Such averages are “portfolios” of forecasts. We characterize the speed and pattern of the gains from diversification as a function of portfolio size (the number of survey respondents) in both (1) the key real-world data-based environment of the U.S. Survey of Professional Forecasters, and (2) the theoretical model-based environment of equicorrelated forecast errors. We proceed by proposing and comparing various direct and model-based “crowd size signature plots,” which summarize the forecasting performance of k-average forecasts as a function of k, where k is the number of forecasts in the average. We then estimate the equicorrelation model for growth and inflation forecast errors by choosing model parameters to minimize the divergence between direct and model-based signature plots. The results indicate near-perfect equicorrelation model fit for both growth and inflation, which we explicate by showing analytically that, under very weak conditions, the direct and fitted equicorrelation model-based signature plots are identical at a particular model parameter configuration. That parameter configuration immediately suggests an analytic closed-form estimator for the direct signature plot, so that equicorrelation ultimately emerges as a device for convenient calculation of direct signature plots, rather than a separate “model” producing separate signature plots. Finally, we find that the gains from survey diversification are greater for inflation forecasts than for growth forecasts, and that they are largely exhausted with inclusion of 5–10 representative forecasters.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Federal Reserve interest rate changes on the stock returns of major U.S. banks over the period from 2005 to 2025. The analysis focuses on six large U.S. banks: JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. Daily stock price data were obtained from Yahoo Finance, and Federal Funds Rate data were collected from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database. Stock returns were calculated using logarithmic returns, and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analysis was used to estimate the relationship between interest rate changes and bank stock returns, while controlling for overall market performance using S&P 500 returns. The empirical results show that Federal Reserve interest rate changes have a statistically significant negative impact on the stock returns of most banks in the sample. Specifically, interest rate increases are associated with declines in stock returns for Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, and Wells Fargo. However, no significant relationship was found for Goldman Sachs. In addition, overall market returns were found to have a strong positive effect on bank stock returns. These findings suggest that monetary policy plays a significant role in influencing bank stock performance and financial market behavior. The results provide important implications for investors, policymakers, and financial institutions in understanding the transmission of monetary policy to the banking sector.

detail.abstract: Nuclear power was once heralded as an inexhaustible, clean, and technologically sophisticated solution to the world's energy demands. Decades of operational history, however, have produced a record of systemic failure, catastrophic risk, and irreversible environmental damage that fundamentally challenges that premise. This paper argues that nuclear power generation has reached the end of its viable lifespan as a global energy source-not because it is impossible to operate safely, but because it is structurally incompatible with the irreducible complexity and unpredictability of the physical world, and because superior alternatives now exist at scale. Drawing on Charles Perrow's Normal Accident Theory, the operational histories of Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, and Fukushima Daiichi, emerging research on long-term ecological contamination, and the economics of renewable energy transition, this paper contends that the case for nuclear power has collapsed on ethical, engineering, economic, and ecological grounds simultaneously. The appropriate policy response is not reform but managed phase-out, with aggressive investment in solar, wind, and grid-scale storage infrastructure. Nuclear energy's moment has passed. Its obsolescence should be recognized, formalized, and acted upon.

title: Implentation of Corporate Criminal Liability Based on Corporate Culture Theory to The Environmental Crime

detail.title: Implentation of Corporate Criminal Liability Based on Corporate Culture Theory to The Environmental Crime
detail.abstract: Corporate criminal liability as regulated under Law Number 32 of 2009 on Environmental Protection and Management and Law Number 39 of 2014 on Plantations still tends to adopt a derivative model of liability. This model attributes the fault of corporate executives to the corporation itself. However, such a model poses difficulties in determining the fault of the individual executives, whether acting alone or collectively. An alternative model of corporate criminal liability is one that identifies the fault inherent within the corporation itself-the Corporate Culture Theory.This study examines the concept and application of corporate criminal liability based on the Corporate Culture Theory in environmental crimes, focusing on the court decision Number 349/Pid.B/LH/2019/PN Plw. The research is a normative legal study, analyzing a court decision that has permanent legal force and is relevant to the research issue, and comparing the contributing factors with those found in another country. Based on the findings, the concept of corporate criminal liability under the Corporate Culture Theory posits that a corporation can be held criminally responsible for its own misconduct, as seen through internal policies, rules, or procedures that result from the corporation's decision-making processes. The application of the Corporate Culture Theory in Decision Number 349/Pid.B/LH/2019/PN Plw is reflected in the judge's consideration of the corporation's non-compliance with its own internal culturespecifically, PT SSS's failure to follow proper procedures for the prevention and control of land and forest fires, which did not meet the required regulatory standards.

detail.abstract: This Article provides the results of an empirical study assessing the determinants of a patent opinion’s influence at the Federal Circuit. I draw on a novel, largely hand-coded dataset of nearly 2,700 decisions issued by the Federal Circuit over a period of more than seven years. I find that some judges are more likely than others to issue binding opinions favoring patent owners (and others favoring patent challengers). In addition, drawing on case citation counts, I find limited evidence that extremely pro-patentee panels tend to write slightly more influential pro-patentee precedential decisions. Perhaps most striking and surprising, however, is how similarly mixed panels (i.e., panelswith at least one pro-patentee judge and at least one pro-challenger judge) decide cases. The results thus support that there’s a moderating impact from having a diversity of viewpoints on a panel. The results also have implications for both the general literature on citation analysis and for assessing the success of the Federal Circuit experiment, including the costs and benefits of vesting so much power in a single court.

detail.abstract: China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is one of the most important geopolitical phenomena of this century. It signals China’s increasing clout overseas while focusing on trade links and infrastructure in general. An important question which has not yet been fully answered is how different countries perceive this initiative, whether they are part of it or not. To answer this question, a large media repository, GDELT, is used to assess each country’s perceptions of the BRI and how they evolve over time. The main finding is that global sentiment on the BRI deteriorated significantly in most geographies from 2017 to 2022, although generally still in positive territory. Further, an empirical analysis is conducted to test the relationship between individual countries’ sentiment towards the BRI and three possible determinants, i.e. economic linkages with China, geopolitical closeness with China, and a country’s perceptions and attitudes about some China-related issues. The results suggest that import dependence on China seems to worsen the image of the BRI. Instead, a country’s geopolitical alignment with China, whether by being a member of the BRI or by voting at the United Nations (UN)like China, is positively correlated with its perceptions of the BRI.

detail.abstract: This paper decomposes welfare measures of policy reforms into parts attributable to redistribution and parts due to efficiency. We further decompose efficiency into subcomponents such as gains from better insurance against idiosyncratic and aggregate risk. Our decomposition of welfare measures associated with alternative feasible allocations is cast in terms of a coordinate system that uses generalized Pareto-Negishi weights to capture inequality and production and consumption wedges to capture distortions. Our decomposition has several desirable properties. It attributes welfare changes from movements along a Pareto frontier to redistribution; it attributes negative efficiency changes to movements away from the Pareto frontier; and it produces subcomponent shares of welfare changes that are numeraire-invariant and symmetric with respect to the direction of the reform. Our decomposition can be explained in terms of an implicit tax-and-transfer system in which redistribution captures real income changes, efficiency captures deadweight losses, and output costs.

title: Well Worth it: Saturated Thickness, Well Capacity, and the Cost of Aquifer Depletion for Irrigated Agriculture
affiliations: Texas A&M University - College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Texas A&M University, University of Georgia, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Texas A&M University

detail.title: Well Worth it: Saturated Thickness, Well Capacity, and the Cost of Aquifer Depletion for Irrigated Agriculture
detail.abstract: We estimate the cost of depleting a natural resource whose value depends jointly on both its stock of quantity and its quality. We study this problem in the context of groundwater by estimating the cost of aquifer depletion for irrigated agriculture in the Colorado portion of the High Plains Aquifer. Using a hedonic valuation approach applied to agricultural land markets, we account for both saturated thickness, the vertical column of water above bedrock, and well capacity, which determines the instantaneous rate at which groundwater can be extracted, a measure of water access quality. We show that, because saturated thickness and well capacity are linked through a nonlinear physical relationship, omitting well capacity from the valuation framework leads to an underestimation of the loss of groundwater wealth from aquifer depletion by 6%. Because well capacity data are often sparse or unavailable, our findings highlight the importance of investments in monitoring infrastructure to accurately value groundwater as natural capital and assess the true cost of depletion.

detail.abstract: Financial markets exhibit highly non-linear, complex dynamics that resist effective characterization by conventional time-series methods. This study introduces and evaluates a fully automated equity trading system grounded in topological data analysis (TDA), a branch of mathematics that quantifies the shape and connectivity of high-dimensional data. The system constructs a sliding-window embedding of S&P 500 price data into point clouds, applies the Vietoris-Rips filtration to produce a nested sequence of simplicial complexes, and computes persistent homology to extract Betti numbers-specifically β 0 (connected components) and β 1 (independent loops)-as proxies for market regime and complexity. A graph Laplacian operator is then applied to the market correlation network to diffuse these topological signals and suppress noise before they are supplied to a Ridge regression model that generates directional trading signals. Backtested on daily equity data spanning January 2021 through early 2026, the Topo + Ridge strategy achieved a cumulative return of approximately 80%, substantially outperforming passive benchmark investment during the same interval. Periods of elevated Betti-0 persistence sum were found to correlate strongly with market stress and high volatility, validating the topological regime-detection hypothesis. These results suggest that persistent homology provides a geometrically meaningful and statistically informative characterization of equity market structure that can be exploited by supervised regression models to generate alpha.

title: Externalities of Geothermal Power Plants: Evidence from Land Prices in Japan
affiliations: Kobe University, Nagoya University and Osaka University of Economics

detail.title: Externalities of Geothermal Power Plants: Evidence from Land Prices in Japan
detail.abstract: Renewable energy deployment faces a fundamental challenge. Climate benefits are globally distributed, whereas economic costs are borne locally by host communities. Despite extensive research quantifying wind power externalities, comparable evidence for geothermal energy, which is a critical baseload renewable resource, remains virtually nonexistent. This study provides the first nationwide quantitative assessment of how geothermal power plants affect local land values. Exploiting a panel dataset covering the period from 1983 to 2024 and all 28 large-scale geothermal installations in Japan, a country with the world's third-largest geothermal potential yet persistent deployment challenges, we employ a difference-in-differences design with spatial fixed effects. Land prices within 2 km of geothermal plants decline by 7 to 12% following installation, effects substantially larger than typical wind turbine impacts (1–6%) and robust across alternative specifications. We show that the aggregate land value losses borne by nearby residents are of a similar order of magnitude to the annual global climate benefits from CO₂ emission reductions, particularly in the early years after installation, revealing pronounced distributional tensions inherent in energy transitions. Our findings provide an empirical foundation for policy frameworks that explicitly address localized economic losses, such as compensation schemes and community benefit-sharing mechanisms, thereby enabling socially and politically feasible geothermal and other place-based renewable energy deployment beyond the Japanese context.

title: Taxing Attention

detail.title: Taxing Attention

publicationDetails.journalName: University of North Carolina Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The rise of social media platforms and other digital businesses has transformed the economy. Companies like Meta and Alphabet have developed a booming industry where advertising revenue drives profits and we, the consumers, provide the product. But what, exactly, are we selling?

For the last decade, the legal and broader academic community has resoundingly categorized this new economy as one focused on data. Consumers use digital platforms like Facebook for “free,” but the platform collects data about the consumer in the process, which is then monetized by selling advertisements. In the realm of tax law, a growing body of work grapples with the complex issues created by the rise of big data. To keep up with any meaningful shift in the economy, a tax system must be able to locate, measure, and subject economic transactions to tax. But digital data is hard to pin down in any meaningful way for tax purposes. How much is our data worth? Where is digital data located geographically? These issues have stymied tax experts across the globe for years.

This Article advocates a fundamental shift in the legal analysis surrounding this new digital economy –particularly the tax law analysis. Specifically, it argues that the primary commodity that is sold to digital platforms by users is not their data; it is their attention. In making this claim, the Article draws on a nascent body of work by economists and other scholars who have argued that the modern economy is more appropriately described as an “attention economy,” rather than one centering on data. The Article argues that transactions between social media companies and users should be reframed as the sale by users of their attention in exchange for the platform’s services. Although data collection is important to the platforms’ businesses, the advertisers ultimately pay for people to pay attention to their ads, not to acquire raw data.

Reframing social media transactions as a sale of consumer attention makes the tax consequences of these exchanges significantly less complex, because the transactions do not involve the sale of a novel intangible asset (digital data). The sale of attention is simply the sale of one’s time—a type of transaction that existed long before digitization. After exploring the tax treatment of the sale of user attention to social media platforms, the Article argues that the monetization of user attention by social media companies merits a policy response. To that end, it proposes a Pigouvian tax on platforms to account for the negative externalities that social media imposes.

title: Identification and Estimation in a Time-Varying Endogenous Random Coefficient Panel Data Model
affiliations: National University of Singapore

detail.title: Identification and Estimation in a Time-Varying Endogenous Random Coefficient Panel Data Model
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a correlated random coefficient linear panel data model, where regressors can be correlated with time-varying and individual-specific random coefficients through both a fixed effect and a time-varying random shock. I develop a new panel data-based method to identify the average partial effect and the local average response function. The identification strategy employs a sufficient statistic to control for the fixed effect and a control variable for the random shock. Conditional on these two controls, the residual variation in the regressors is driven solely by the exogenous instrumental variables, and thus can be exploited to identify the parameters of interest. The constructive identification analysis leads to three-step series estimators, for which I establish rates of convergence and asymptotic normality. To illustrate the method, I estimate a heterogeneous Cobb-Douglas production function for manufacturing firms in China, finding substantial variations in output elasticities across firms that can be related to various firm characteristics.

title: Initial-Condition-Robust Inference in Autoregressive Models
affiliations: National University of Singapore, Yale University - Cowles Foundation and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Initial-Condition-Robust Inference in Autoregressive Models
detail.abstract: This paper considers confidence intervals (CIs) for the autoregressive (AR) parameter in an AR model with an AR parameter that may be close or equal to one. Existing CIs rely on the assumption of a stationary or fixed initial condition to obtain correct asymptotic coverage and good finite sample coverage. When this assumption fails, their coverage can be quite poor. In this paper, we introduce a new CI for the AR parameter whose coverage probability is completely robust to the initial condition, both asymptotically and in finite samples. This CI pays only a small price in terms of its length when the initial condition is stationary or fixed. The new CI also is robust to conditional heteroskedasticity of the errors.

detail.title: How Close Is China’s Medium-Term Outlook to That of Japan? An Economic-Historical Perspective

publicationDetails.detailsText: Financial and Economic Review, volume 24, issue 3, 2025[10.33893/FER.24.3.23]

detail.abstract: After decades of strong growth, China’s economy began a steady slowdown around 2012. Current GDP growth is less than half of previous levels, and the trend is expected to continue. Since its real estate bubble burst in mid-2021, deflationary pressures have raised concerns that China may follow Japan’s trajectory from the early 1990s. Both countries show similar structural traits: low private consumption, high savings and significant economic imbalances – China’s even more so. Their policy responses have also mirrored each other: slow monetary and fiscal easing, focus on manufacturing and reliance on trade surpluses, prompting US protectionist reactions. Like Japan, China is offshoring production to counteract trade barriers. However, China differs in key ways: it is still a developing economy with more room for growth and is a far stronger geopolitical force than Japan was. This power both motivates US technological restrictions and gives China broader global leverage, especially in the Global South. Whether China will repeat Japan’s path remains a crucial, open question.

title: A Bibliometric Analysis of Sustainable Finance Instruments for Small and Medium Size Enterprises
